text:
Strategic alliances are instruments of deterrence, not mechanisms for automatic escalation.
Taking a nation to war against a nuclear-armed state on the basis of an act by a non-state actor, without credible attribution, state responsibility and clear evidence, would be strategically reckless. Terrorism can involve proxies, third parties or even false flag operations; therefore, attribution must precede escalation.
The Makkah Pact should similarly be understood in its proper strategic context: collective deterrence against a structured state threat to the sovereignty, territorial integrity or vital security interests of a member, not automatic mobilization of the entire alliance after every action by  Houthis or any other non-state actor.
Saudi Arabia possesses substantial national military capability to address such threats. Invoking the entire alliance prematurely would dilute rather than strengthen its credibility.
A serious alliance must distinguish between terrorism, proxy action and direct state aggression.
Credible deterrence requires capability. Strategic deterrence requires judgment.

text:
The Mecca Pact, signed 7 August 2026 by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan, is a trilateral mutual-defense agreement.

Core clause: an armed attack on one member is treated as an attack on all three — conceptually similar to NATO Article 5, but without a published full text, standing command, or detailed trigger procedures.

Why it matters:

Combines Pakistan’s nuclear deterrent, Saudi energy and financial weight, and Türkiye’s NATO membership plus defense industry

Builds on the 2025 Saudi-Pakistan Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement

Comes amid regional instability and questions about external security guarantees

What’s still unknown: exact definition of “armed attack,” mandatory vs optional assistance, geographic scope, and how decisions get made.

Possible first test: Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Pakistan has said the pact could apply if Saudi territory is hit, while drawing a line at joining operations inside Yemen.

Egypt, Syria, Qatar, and Bangladesh have been mentioned as possible future members. For now it remains a three-state arrangement with plans for joint exercises and defense-industry cooperation.

Not a “Muslim NATO” yet — more a new, untested collective-defense pledge whose real meaning will be written in the next crisis.

By launching ballistic missiles and drones into Saudi Arabia itself, striking around Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, the Houthis have created the first serious test of the month-old Mecca Joint Defense Agreement between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey.

Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif has already warned that unprovoked spillover onto Saudi territory could make the agreement operational, saying Pakistan would honor its commitments if required.

And this red line predates the new pact.

🛡️ In 2015, Pakistan refused to enter the Yemen war but explicitly drew the line at attacks on Saudi territory. The Houthis have now crossed precisely that threshold.

🛡️ Pakistani forces are already stationed in Saudi Arabia. Pakistan would not need to invade Yemen. Additional air defenses, intelligence support, drones or limited strikes against Houthi launch sites in northern Yemen could constitute meaningful involvement.

🛡️ Saudi Arabia is economically critical to Pakistan, through deposits, oil arrangements and billions in remittances. Signing a defense agreement and then doing nothing after Saudi territory is attacked would carry its own political and strategic cost.

🛡️ Pakistan also has major maritime and energy interests at stake. Continued Houthi escalation around the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb directly threatens shipping and energy routes important to Pakistan.

They are already facing renewed advances by Yemeni government forces on multiple fronts. Adding Pakistan’s large, nuclear-armed military to the forces opposing them would dramatically widen the pressure they are facing.

It would also create a serious problem for the Islamic Republic. Pakistan has spent considerable effort balancing relations with Iran against its deep security and economic relationship with Saudi Arabia. An Iranian proxy attacking Saudi territory forces Pakistan toward a choice the Islamic Republic would rather it never have to make.

And if Pakistan does nothing, the alternative is damaging in a completely different way.

The Mecca Pact risks being exposed as paper during its first major test.

The Houthis have therefore turned another missile attack into something much bigger.

Either they help drag Pakistan into the war against them, or they expose one of the region’s newest mutual-defense agreements as hollow.

They may have fired at Saudi Arabia, but the consequences could reach far beyond it.

The Houthis are Iran’s Yemen file. Pakistan has spent years not picking that fight. Turkey has its own line to Tehran. Reuters says Islamabad already walked a Saudi warning into Iran: pull the leash. The stumble Mario named.
Almost nobody in that triangle wants a three-front Islamic-world war. Alliances do not ask what you want. They ask what you signed. 🇵🇰🇾🇪 Pakistan has just warned that it could enter the Yemen war to defend Saudi Arabia. This is how regional wars stop being regional.

After the biggest Houthi attacks on Saudi in years, Pakistan's defense minister says there should be "no doubt" about Islamabad's obligations under the Mecca defense pact.

An attack on one member is considered an attack on all three: Pakistan, Saudi, and Turkey.

The problem is who Pakistan may now have to fight.

The Houthis are aligned with Iran, and Pakistan has spent years carefully building its relationship with Tehran. Turkey has done the same.

But if Houthi missiles continue hitting Saudi territory, that balancing act could become impossible. Pakistani officials have already travelled to Istanbul for talks as the crisis intensifies.

And Iran doesn't necessarily need to attack Pakistan or Turkey directly.

It can pour more support into the Houthis, increase pressure on Saudi and help turn Bab el-Mandeb into another economic chokepoint while Hormuz is already under enormous strain.

That's what makes this so dangerous.

Almost nobody involved appears to actually want this wider war, but alliances have consequences.

One Houthi attack triggers a Saudi response; they invoke their allies, Pakistan or Turkey enters Yemen, then Iran decides it can't abandon the Houthis.

And suddenly everyone discovers they've stumbled into a war they were desperately trying to avoid.

The Middle East doesn't need another country to decide it wants a bigger war; it just needs the next country to decide it has no choice but to join the one already burning.

text:
The Mecca Pact is insurance paperwork, not a war-winning machine.
Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan signed “an attack on one is an attack on all” after the 2026 Iran war showed two things: Gulf plants can burn, and the US umbrella is no longer treated as automatic. Article-5 language with no published triggers, no C2 and no force tables is consultation. Jazan after the signature proved it.
Look at the signatories, not the communiqué. Pakistan is already trapped in its own fiscal, political and India-facing mess; a Gulf clause does not conjure spare combat power. Türkiye can raise defence spending and sell drones; that is not the same as underwriting a Red Sea war. Saudi Arabia is still entangled with the Houthis while the Iran war continues. None of that is solved by a secretariat in Riyadh.
Same fortnight: SCO condemns strikes on Iran and hands Pakistan the chair. BRICS this weekend seats Riyadh and Tehran under an Indian host. Overlapping clubs. Divergent threat maps.
Hedging, not a bloc. Treat “Sunni NATO” and “post-American order” as slogan analysis. Alliances in this region die when they cannot answer four questions they left blank: against whom, with what, where, at whose cost.

THE SIGNIFICANCE OF THE VENUE: MECCA

By choosing the birthplace of Islam, the signatories are not just signing a document; they are making a sacred covenant. This transforms a political alliance into a religious obligation, making it significantly harder to break or challenge. As one analyst noted, the timing and setting "sent a message to other Muslim leaders and, above all, their own populations that this was not simply a political agreement, but a sacred one" . This is a strategic masterstroke, as it co-opts religious legitimacy for a geopolitical project.

THE IMPLICATIONS FOR REGIONAL CONFLICT

The shift in psychology could be decisive. The Abraham Accords were ultimately transactional—a deal between governments. The Mecca Pact, by contrast, has the potential to mobilize populations on religious grounds. This is the missing piece in many Western analyses. By framing the pact in religious terms, it becomes a moral and spiritual duty to defend its signatories. If a conflict were to arise, support for the pact could be framed as a defense of faith, not just politics. This fundamentally alters the cost-benefit analysis for any potential aggressor. The pact also represents a direct challenge to the Abraham Accords, positioning the bloc as a counterweight to U.S.-Israeli influence in the region.

text:
Reaching an agreement is quite easy; however, maintaining and implementing that agreement requires sincerity and strong will from both parties. The fact that international agreements are made and broken repeatedly demonstrates the importance of this condition.

The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) was a regional political and economic union of 15 West African countries; Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger have since withdrawn. It was established by the former colonial powers France and Portugal with the aim of creating an African Economic Community, similar to the European Economic Community (which formed the basis of the EU), and eventually evolving into a political structure like the EU; however, today it exists only on paper. 

The Sahel States Alliance was formed by Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger with the ambition of encompassing the entire “Sahel” belt from the Atlantic to the Red Sea, but it has remained a common market among these three countries.

The bilateral alliances of the United States with Japan, South Korea, and the Philippines, the Collective Security Treaty Organization (organized by Russia to replace the Soviet Union, and including Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Armenia), and the separate alliances of North Korea, Russia, and China, have not been able to become effective, influential, and long-lasting organizations like NATO. In fact, there is no other alliance like NATO; nor is there any effort to create one.

As Tekin Öget, a writer for TürkTime, a key element of our media for 23 years with his exclusive reports and commentary, points out, the Mecca agreement differs from previous ones in one respect: “In the vision of the Mecca Pact, which symbolizes the Ankara-Mecca-Islamabad security axis, a geographical giant, Türkiye, is included.”

The agreement reached between these three countries, symbolizing solidarity and a security axis in the Islamic world, is truly an unprecedented alliance. This agreement replaces the bilateral agreement between Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed approximately a year ago, and was expanded on Friday, August 7th, at the Safa Palace in Mecca to include Türkiye’s defense industry and its army built to NATO standards.

The signed text stated, “The States Parties undertake to consider any act of aggression against one of them as an act against all of the parties”; however, statements made by President Erdoğan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shahbaz Sharif indicate that this “collective security pact” is open to other countries as well. The first committee established under the agreement, the “Strategic Political and Defence Committee,” held its first meeting in Istanbul earlier this week. The meeting was attended by the foreign and defence ministers and chiefs of staff of the three founding countries. At the meeting, it was decided that the organization’s official name would be the “Mecca Defence Pact,” that its governing secretariat would be established in Riyadh, and that the first secretary-general would be Pakistani.

Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan reiterated that the alliance is based on “international principles such as respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of other states and non-interference in their internal affairs,” and stated that any country in the region could join the pact. The meeting, held just hours after hostilities resumed between Washington and Tehran following a month-long truce, led to speculation that the call for new members was directed at Iran.

However, it should not be forgotten that the Mecca Agreement was signed while the Gaza Genocide, which began on October 7th, and the war with Iran, launched by the US and Israel on February 28th, were ongoing. Not only Iran, but also the Middle East and the Islamic world, especially Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar, and Egypt, are affected and even targeted by these two events.

text:
Few countries have Bangladesh’s particular combination of geography and history. Born in 1971 after a devastating war of liberation, Bangladesh emerged as a sovereign state on the eastern edge of the Indian subcontinent, surrounded on three sides by India and bounded to the south by the Bay of Bengal. To its southeast lies Myanmar, while the country's maritime interests increasingly connect it to the wider Indian Ocean and Indo-Pacific.

That geography has never been merely a map. It has shaped Bangladesh's security thinking from independence onwards.

The country inherited difficult strategic realities: a long and complex land border with India, a strategically important coastline and maritime domain, proximity to the Bay of Bengal's major sea lanes, and a position between two of Asia's most consequential powers, India and China. Its historical experience has also left a deep imprint on the relationship between political authority, the state and the armed forces.

Over the past five and a half decades, Bangladesh has experienced periods of military rule, military intervention in politics, civilian governments operating amid substantial military influence, and periods in which civilian and military institutions have functioned largely within separate spheres. The armed forces have simultaneously become one of the country's most important national institutions — respected for their role in national defence, disaster response and international peacekeeping — while remaining politically sensitive because of the country's history.

This is the context in which Bangladesh must now reconsider how it makes decisions about national security.

The strategic environment surrounding Bangladesh is changing rapidly. India remains its most important geographical neighbour, China has become a major economic and defence partner, and Bangladesh's engagement with the United States, Japan, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and other states is expanding. The Bay of Bengal is becoming increasingly important to regional commerce and strategic competition, while developments in the Indo-Pacific are bringing new economic, technological and military considerations into Dhaka's calculations.

At the same time, Bangladesh is contemplating major decisions about defence modernisation, advanced combat aircraft, naval capabilities, air defence, unmanned systems and other military technologies. 

Questions surrounding possible participation in new security arrangements, including the recently signed Mecca Pact, further demonstrate how closely defence policy, diplomacy and national strategy have become intertwined.

Yet Bangladesh's institutional machinery for making such decisions has not evolved at the same pace as the country's strategic importance.

This is why Jon Danilowicz's intervention deserves serious consideration.

He raises an important and long-overdue question: who actually makes Bangladesh's national-security policy, on what basis, and within what institutional framework?

His argument is particularly relevant because Bangladesh does not simply need stronger armed forces. It needs a stronger national-security decision-making system capable of determining what those armed forces are required to achieve, how military capabilities should be prioritised, and how defence policy fits within the country's wider diplomatic, economic and strategic interests.

That distinction is critical.

Bangladesh's national-security challenge is no longer simply a question of military preparedness. It encompasses diplomacy, economic resilience, energy security, maritime interests, cyber security, technology, intelligence, critical infrastructure and the country's ability to maintain strategic autonomy in an increasingly competitive region.

The question before Bangladesh, therefore, is not whether the military should have more or less influence.

It is whether Bangladesh has the institutions necessary to ensure that political leaders receive professional, independent and comprehensive advice before making decisions that may shape the country's security for decades.

text:
The Mecca Pact as the Real Benchmark

Analysts focused exclusively on the SCO aspiration are missing the strategically more consequential development: the August 7, 2026 Mecca Joint Defense Agreement between Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan [Source: CFR, August 2026]. Where the SCO membership is aspirational, the Mecca pact is done. It is signed, it creates mutual defence obligations, and it institutionalises what CFR describes as Erdoğan's "ideological commitment" to a "Muslim NATO" [Source: CFR, August 2026].

The pact's strategic geometry is worth mapping precisely because it does not move as a unitary actor. Saudi Arabia joined primarily to hedge against U.S. unreliability, demonstrated during the Iranian drone strikes of 2019 and, more recently, the Israeli attack on Doha in September 2025. Pakistan joined to enhance its influence in the Gulf at India's expense. Turkey joined to expand its regional leadership role and give institutional form to its Islamist-adjacent foreign policy identity. These three motivations are compatible in the short run but create coalition fracture points at the medium horizon: Riyadh and Islamabad have no shared interest in Turkey's European ambitions, and Turkey has no shared interest in Pakistani-Indian dynamics.

The pact's most immediate cross-domain consequence is the proposed IMEC redirection. Turkey and Saudi Arabia have proposed rerouting the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor away from Jordan-Israel toward a Syria-Turkey axis [Source: CFR, August 2026]. If this materialises, it would deprive Israel of a critical connectivity dividend from the Abraham Accords and deny India the direct Gulf-Europe corridor that underpins its own great-power positioning. Washington invested political capital in IMEC as the non-China alternative to Belt and Road; Turkey's participation in its proposed disruption is therefore a direct challenge to a U.S. strategic infrastructure priority.

text:
Pakistan must transform human resources into economic strength: Ahsan Iqbal

 LAHORE : Federal Minister for Planning, Development and Special Initiatives Ahsan Iqbal said on Thursday that Pakistan’s path to development lies through education, research, innovation and technology, stressing the need to empower the country’s youth and transform its human resources into economic strength.
Addressing a conference on “The Makkah Pact & the New Geometry of Power” at the University of Lahore, where he was the chief guest, the minister said Pakistan must move towards a knowledge-based and production-oriented economy by strengthening linkages between universities and industry.
The conference was attended by political and former military officials, bureaucrats, journalists and members of the business community.
Ahsan Iqbal said the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement should not be viewed merely as a military arrangement but as a broader framework encompassing universities, laboratories, technology, investment, connectivity and economic cooperation.
He said the changing global landscape had enhanced the significance of the agreement signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye in Makkah on August 7, https://t.co/aqjs6Bflio Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan signed the agreement, he added.
The minister said its basic principle was that an attack on one member would be considered an attack on all, adding that the pact should not be seen as a challenge to the global system but as a step towards a more stable regional and international order.
He said Saudi Arabia had vast economic resources, energy strength, financial capacity and growing ambitions in technology, while Turkiye possessed a strong industrial base, an advanced defence industry and an important geographical position linking Europe, Asia and the Middle East.
Pakistan, he said, had a large young population, significant defence capabilities and strategic geographical importance, connecting South Asia, Central Asia, China, the Arabian Sea and the Gulf.
“The real importance of the Makkah Pact does not lie only in combining the military capabilities of three countries,” he said, adding that it could provide a foundation for cooperation in joint defence production, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, space technology, energy, food security and critical minerals.
Ahsan Iqbal said Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia should strengthen partnerships in research, investment and regional connectivity, adding that combining Pakistani human capital, Turkish technology and Saudi investment could bring about significant transformation.
He stressed that geopolitics must be linked with geo-economics and said Pakistan’s objective should be strategic autonomy, not strategic isolation.
“Pakistan’s strategic thinking is based on friendship with all and dependence on none,” he said, adding that Islamabad wanted peaceful and mutually beneficial relations with all neighbouring countries, as well as stronger partnerships with China, the United States, Europe and the Muslim world.
The minister said military strength alone could not make a country powerful, as a weak economy, imported technology, ineffective institutions and poor education could also undermine national security.
He said the foundations of national strength included economic productivity, technology, human capital and social cohesion.
Ahsan Iqbal said Pakistan’s next major national struggle would be fought through exports, education and technology rather than fighter aircraft, describing it as a “battle for development”.
He said Pakistan needed to transform its population into economic strength by producing scientists, engineers, entrepreneurs, skilled workers and exporters.

Dr. Abdulaziz Sager argues that the Mecca Pact strengthens #SaudiArabia’s deterrence, defence capabilities and strategic autonomy by deepening cooperation with #Türkiye and #Pakistan. The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement reflects an important evolution in #SaudiArabia’s security strategy, strengthening deterrence, expanding strategic depth, and building greater national defence capacity.

In his latest contribution, GRC Chairman Dr. Abdulaziz Sager argues that the pact with Türkiye and Pakistan should be understood not as a strategic realignment, but as part of a broader Saudi approach to diversifying security partnerships while maintaining the United States and the GCC as central pillars of the Kingdom’s security architecture.

The agreement’s long-term significance may lie as much in what it helps Saudi Arabia build as in its collective defence commitment: deeper military coordination, stronger air and missile defence, counter-drone and maritime capabilities, technology transfer, defence industrialisation, and greater preparedness for an increasingly complex regional threat environment.

Ultimately, the Mecca Pact points to greater Saudi strategic agency—an approach in which Riyadh is not simply participating in regional security arrangements, but increasingly developing the capabilities and partnerships needed to shape them.

The Mecca Pact should not be viewed as an alternative to the GCC security framework, but rather as an additional layer within it.

Gulf security remains structurally interconnected across its airspace, maritime routes, energy infrastructure, and critical supply chains. This makes the #GCC an indispensable element of Saudi Arabia’s regional security calculations.

Paul Craig Roberts

There have been some surprising new developments recently, implying significant shifts in the balance of power. These developments have largely gone unnoticed, and their implications have not been analyzed. I've attempted to do so in online interviews at Dialogue Works and On Target . This combination of redefining the conflict and propaganda constitutes Trump's exit strategy.

This development combines conventional military force with oil reserves and nuclear weapons and unites three distinct Muslim ethnic groups in a strategic location with a population of 355,390,000. These people are largely Sunni Muslims.

Another development is the announcement in Iranian media that Iran, a Shiite majority, has been invited to join the alliance. If true, this would indicate that the Sunni-Shiite schism is fading. It would also mean a pact between four countries with a population of 448.7 million, larger than the United States, with conventional and nuclear power, a significant share of the world's oil reserves, and control over strategic oil waterways. This would be a strategically important bloc for Russia and China, as the geographical location of the pact of four Muslim countries protects Russian and Chinese interests. Such a pact could become a de facto alliance of six countries.

These developments, if real and not just words, mark the end of any pretense of American hegemony and the Israeli project of a "Greater Israel." Israel's population of 10 million, of which only 7.8 million are Jews, is dwarfed by the 448.7 million Muslims. Furthermore, the protection offered by the alliance would likely lead to the accession of Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, Iraq, and Yemen, and an end to the wars fomented by Washington among Muslims. Syria itself could be reconstituted, and Israel could be forced to return enough of Palestine to make a two-state solution possible.

Such an opportunity has not presented itself to Muslims for centuries, and the opportunity is so extraordinary that it seems destined to slip away due to stupidity, incompetence, and petty squabbling.

It's possible that Netanyahu's coalition will be ousted in the next elections. This possibility could increase significantly if Iran were to receive and accept an invitation to join the Mecca Pact, as this would demonstrate to the Israelis that the Zionist project of "Greater Israel" is no longer viable and that an agreement must be reached with the Muslim Middle East. If peace were to come to the Middle East, it could perhaps come elsewhere as well.

H10 — THE HOSTILE TEN
I am expanding my political dismantling list from H9 to H10.
The tenth organization is the Non-Aligned Movement — NAM.
My H10 list is now:
SCO • BRICS • OPEC • CSTO • EAEU • CIS • G20 • OIC • MECCA PACT • NAM
By “dismantle” I mean peaceful political, economic and institutional deconstruction — never military violence.
These organizations are very different from one another. Some are military alliances, some economic blocs, some diplomatic forums and some commodity organizations. But in my view they share one increasingly important problem: they can provide alternative structures through which authoritarian powers, revisionist regimes and governments hostile to the Euro-Atlantic order coordinate, gain legitimacy or reduce Western influence.

The answer of the Free World must not be war.

The answer must be competition, isolation of aggressors, economic derisking and better institutions.

Europe and the democratic world must offer sovereign states a more attractive future:

🇪🇺 stronger EU integration
🛡️ stronger NATO cooperation
🌍 stronger OECD structures
🤝 deeper democratic partnerships
💶 access to prosperous Western markets
⚡ energy independence from authoritarian suppliers
🌐 investment, connectivity and free trade
🕊️ sovereignty without imperial spheres of influence

Why add the Non-Aligned Movement?

Because in 2026, “non-alignment” is increasingly an outdated geopolitical concept.

The world is not living in 1961.

Europe faces a major security confrontation. Russia is waging war against Ukraine. China is building an alternative geopolitical architecture. Iran and other authoritarian regimes increasingly cooperate against Western interests.

In this environment, celebrating “non-alignment” can become an excuse for refusing strategic choices.

And nowhere is this contradiction clearer than in Serbia.

Serbia says it wants European Union membership while simultaneously celebrating the old Yugoslav tradition of Non-Alignment and maintaining deep political relations with states outside the Euro-Atlantic system.

That contradiction cannot continue forever.

Serbia must choose Europe — not geopolitical nostalgia.

EU membership means strategic convergence with Europe. It means alignment with European foreign and security policy. It means accepting that Serbia's future is with its European neighbours, not in recreating Tito-era diplomacy between competing power blocs.

The same principle applies globally.

I do not oppose countries because they are Chinese, Russian, Indian, Arab, Muslim, Asian, African or Latin American.

I oppose geopolitical structures when they strengthen authoritarian power, imperial spheres of influence, energy coercion or systematic opposition to the democratic world.

My strategy for H10 is therefore:

ISOLATE AGGRESSORS.
DERISK ECONOMICALLY.
ATTRACT DEMOCRACIES.
OFFER BETTER ALTERNATIVES.
STRENGTHEN EU–NATO–OECD COOPERATION.
PEACEFULLY DISMANTLE THE H10.

The Free World must organize itself again.

BUILD A STRONGER FREE-WORLD ORDER.

Günther Fehlinger-Jahn
Chairman, Austrian Committee for NATO Enlargement

Larry Johnson: Not an Islamic NATO; The Mecca Agreement Is Building the Post-American Security Architecture — and Iran Is About to Walk In https://t.co/Q5UWvfZtJS 
The Western commentariat filed the Mecca agreement under a comfortable heading. When Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement on August 7 — an armed attack on one to be treated as an attack on all — the reflexive label was “Islamic NATO,” a Sunni bloc, three of the Muslim world’s largest militaries welded together by sectarian identity. That reading was obsolete almost before the ink dried. What is actually taking shape is not a Sunni alliance against Iran. It is the first load-bearing beam of the post-American security architecture that Russia and China have been calling for — and Tehran is about to walk through the door.

The language was not accidental, and it did not originate in Riyadh. On April 27, in St. Petersburg, after meeting Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Vladimir Putin called for a new security architecture in the Persian Gulf. One week later, on May 5–6 in Beijing, after his own meeting with Araghchi, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said essentially the same thing — that Beijing supports the establishment of a regional peace and security architecture in which the regional countries themselves participate, safeguard common interests, and pursue common development. Araghchi, for his part, told Putin that Iran supports a new post-war regional architecture that can coordinate development and security.

Note the two nouns Araghchi paired: development and security. That pairing is the tell, and I will return to it. Russia has floated a collective security concept for the Gulf since 2019; Lavrov reiterated it on February 28, 2026 — the very day the war began. The consistent aim is a multilateral, regionally led framework that replaces the American defense umbrella over the Gulf, installs Moscow and Beijing as the guarantors alongside the regional states, and — crucially — treats Iran not as a threat to be contained but as a legitimate pillar of the order. As Araghchi paraphrased his Chinese hosts: Iran after the war is a different country, its standing improved, a new era of cooperation ahead.

Hold that blueprint in mind, and look again at Mecca.

The first pillar
The Makkah agreement was signed in wartime, and that context is everything. Nearly six months into the war that began on February 28, Saudi Arabia had absorbed repeated missile and drone strikes, and confidence in Washington’s willingness to actually backstop Gulf security in real time had visibly cracked. Out of that erosion came a treaty binding Pakistan — the only nuclear-armed Muslim state, with an arsenal near 300 warheads — to Turkey, which fields NATO’s second-largest army, and to Saudi Arabia, the Gulf’s financial anchor and custodian of Islam’s holiest cities. Nearly 1.4 million active personnel and some $124 billion in combined annual defense spending, joined under a single mutual-defense formula for the first time since the Baghdad Pact era.

The signatories were careful to call it purely defensive and, in Erdogan’s words, open to other countries. Ankara floated Egypt; Dhaka signaled interest. The Western analysts who noted that all three members are American partners — Turkey in NATO, Pakistan a major non-NATO ally, Saudi Arabia the largest buyer of U.S. arms — and concluded the pact was therefore no threat to Washington, made the same error as those who called it a Sunni NATO. They read the founding membership and missed the trajectory. A pact “open to others,” signed by states that have lost faith in the American umbrella, in the middle of a war against Iran that Iran is surviving, was never going to stay a three-member Sunni club.

Here is what the public analysis has not yet caught up to, and what I can report from firsthand sources. On Monday morning, Field Marshal Asim Munir — Pakistan’s chief of army staff and the real architect of Islamabad’s regional strategy — is in Iran. The subject of his talks is Iran’s accession to the Mecca agreement as its fourth member.

Read that slowly, because it detonates the entire “Islamic NATO” framing. A mutual-defense pact led by the Sunni heavyweights of the Muslim world, admitting Shia Iran, is not a sectarian bloc. It is the opposite: the dissolution of the very Sunni-Shia fault line that Western strategy has exploited for a generation. And what remains, once Iran is inside, is not “NATO” of any confessional flavor. It is precisely the inclusive, regionally led architecture that Putin and Wang Yi described — a framework in which Iran sits as a legitimate pillar rather than a quarantined enemy. Mecca provided the structure. Tehran’s entry supplies the meaning.

It does not stop at Iran. Bahrain — a Gulf monarchy that hosts the U.S. Fifth Fleet — is, I am told, negotiating with Pakistan to join the military alliance with Saudi Arabia. Consider the weight of that. The Gulf state most physically entangled with American naval power is hedging toward the regional bloc. Each such accession chips another brick out of the American security order in the Gulf and mortars it into the new structure rising beside it.

Recall Araghchi’s pairing — development and security. A security architecture that does not carry an economic circulatory system is a paper alliance. The Mecca pact is acquiring one, and here again Pakistan is the hinge.

Islamabad — with China standing behind it, through the CPEC investment and the Gwadar port that already give Pakistan its overland corridors into Iran — has decided to deepen its economic integration with Tehran dramatically. Munir is negotiating a tenfold increase in Pakistan-Iran trade over three years. That is not a rounding error in a sanctions regime. It is a demolition of one.

And it is, to put it plainly, a slap across the face of Scott Bessent. The US Treasury Secretary has spent the war promising the toughest sanctions in history, an unprecedented campaign to isolate Iran economically and starve it into capitulation. He is now watching a nuclear-armed American ally, financed and backed by China, move to multiply its trade with the very country he vows to strangle — trade that will run on yuan and barter and regional currencies, outside the dollar clearing system his sanctions depend on. The security architecture and the economic architecture are being built in the same motion, by the same man, on the same trip. Bessent’s isolation strategy is being answered not with defiance in words but with integration in deeds.

There is a deeper irony here, and it is worth naming, because it indicts a generation of American strategy. For decades Washington treated the Sunni-Shia divide as an asset to be worked — arming and tolerating Sunni militants as instruments against Shia Iran, from the redirection of the Bush years through the Syrian war. The entire logic depended on the divide staying open. Now the principal Sunni powers of the region — Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan — are themselves closing it, folding Iran into a shared framework of defense and commerce. The wedge Washington spent twenty years driving is becoming the foundation of a bloc that answers to Moscow and Beijing rather than to Washington. That is blowback of the highest order: not a weapon turned on its maker, but a fault line the maker relied upon, sealing shut.

An opinion is not worth much if it cannot survive its own qualifications, so here they are. Munir’s trip is a negotiation, not a signing; Iran’s accession and Bahrain’s are, as of this writing, in motion, not concluded, and either could stall. The Sunni-Shia trust deficit is real and decades deep — Gulf monarchies have long feared Iranian subversion, and a defense treaty does not erase that overnight. Prior mutual-defense pacts in the region, including the Saudi-Pakistani agreement of September 2025 and the older GCC arrangements, never once triggered a NATO-style collective response, and this one may prove as declaratory as those. All three Mecca signatories retain deep, live relationships with the United States and will not sever them lightly; much of this may be hedging rather than a clean break. And the firsthand reporting above describes intentions and negotiations, which are not yet treaties.

But direction is not the same as arrival, and direction is unmistakable. Every one of these hedges points the same way — away from the American umbrella and toward a regional order underwritten by Russia and China.

The Mecca agreement was sold to Western audiences as a Sunni bloc and dismissed as a club of American clients. It is neither. It is the first pillar of the security architecture Putin and Wang Yi named this spring after sitting with Iran’s foreign minister — a regionally led, Russia- and China-backed framework that folds Iran in as a legitimate power and pushes the United States out as the indispensable one. When Asim Munir walks into Tehran on Monday to discuss Iran’s membership, and negotiates a tenfold expansion of trade in the same breath, he is not conducting two errands. He is laying two courses of the same wall. The Americans built their Gulf position on keeping Sunni and Shia apart and keeping the dollar in the middle. Both pillars are being pulled at once — and the structure going up in their place was drawn in Moscow and Beijing.

text:
I have read Jon Danilowicz’s assessment of the possibility of Bangladesh joining the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement with interest. He raises several legitimate questions, particularly regarding military commitments, interoperability and the implications for Bangladesh’s relations with India.

However, I believe some of the concerns in his analysis need to be put into a more practical military context.

1. Interoperability is not the major problem it is being made out to be

The argument that Bangladesh would face significant interoperability problems with the other members is, in my view, overstated.

Bangladesh, Pakistan, Türkiye and Saudi Arabia do not operate four completely different military ecosystems. There is already considerable overlap.

Bangladesh and Pakistan are particularly relevant in this regard. Both operate large numbers of Chinese-origin weapons and platforms, including combat aircraft, armoured vehicles, artillery, air-defence systems and naval equipment. Pakistan has obviously gone much further down this road, but the basic familiarity with Chinese systems already exists within the Bangladesh Armed Forces.

At the same time, all four countries operate significant quantities of Western or NATO-standard equipment.

Türkiye is a NATO member and has decades of experience operating within NATO structures. Saudi Arabia operates a predominantly Western-equipped force. Pakistan has extensive experience operating American systems alongside Chinese platforms. Bangladesh itself has a mixed inventory containing Chinese, Western and other foreign-origin equipment.

Modern military interoperability does not require everyone to fly the same aircraft or operate the same tank.

What matters is whether forces can communicate, exchange information, coordinate fires, operate under compatible command arrangements and sustain one another in a joint operation.

Those are training and institutional problems. They are not insurmountable obstacles.

2. Bangladesh already knows how to operate in multinational environments

There is another factor that should not be overlooked.

The Bangladesh Armed Forces have been involved in UN peacekeeping for decades. Bangladeshi officers and troops have worked with militaries from Europe, Asia, Africa, the Middle East and the Americas, often under multinational command arrangements.

This is not a military that is unfamiliar with operating alongside foreign forces.

If anything, Bangladesh's peacekeeping experience gives it a useful foundation for developing the joint procedures required by a new defence arrangement.

The difference would be that the Mecca Pact could take this experience beyond the largely peacekeeping environment and into structured defence cooperation, joint exercises, intelligence-sharing and contingency planning.

3. Pakistan is probably the easiest interoperability partner for Bangladesh

This point deserves more attention than it usually receives.

Of all the potential members, Pakistan is arguably the country with which Bangladesh could develop military interoperability most naturally.

Both countries operate substantial Chinese-origin inventories. The Pakistan Air Force has extensive experience with Chinese combat aircraft and weapons, while Bangladesh operates Chinese fighters and other Chinese systems as the backbone of several parts of its force structure.

There is therefore a degree of commonality in equipment, technical knowledge and operating concepts that should not be dismissed.

Bangladesh does not have to start from scratch.

4. Türkiye and Saudi Arabia add capabilities that Bangladesh needs

The more interesting issue is what Bangladesh could gain.

Türkiye has built a serious defence-industrial base and has developed considerable expertise in UAVs, missiles, electronic warfare, naval systems and indigenous weapons production.

Saudi Arabia brings substantial financial resources, advanced Western-origin military equipment and access to the Gulf's strategic environment.

Pakistan brings scale, operational experience and a major defence relationship with China.

For Bangladesh, these relationships could potentially translate into training, technology, defence-industrial cooperation, intelligence cooperation and access to capabilities that would otherwise take much longer to develop.

That should be part of the calculation.

5. Bangladesh needs a deterrence strategy

This is where I think the discussion needs to go beyond interoperability.

Bangladesh sits between two very different security problems.

India is overwhelmingly the dominant military power in South Asia and surrounds Bangladesh on three sides. Myanmar, meanwhile, remains a significant security concern on Bangladesh's south-eastern flank.

Bangladesh therefore needs a credible deterrence posture towards both India and Myanmar.

That does not mean Bangladesh is preparing for war with either country.

It means ensuring that neither country can ever conclude that Bangladesh is sufficiently weak or isolated that military coercion would be a low-risk proposition.

That distinction is fundamental.

The purpose of deterrence is to prevent a war from starting in the first place.

6. Bangladesh cannot compete with India through numbers

Nobody seriously argues that Bangladesh should attempt to match India platform-for-platform.

India's population, economy, defence budget and industrial base make that impossible and unnecessary.

Bangladesh has to take a different approach.

It needs a capable military built around survivability, precision, air and maritime denial, intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, modern communications and, above all, the ability to impose unacceptable costs on an aggressor.

External partnerships can add another layer to that deterrence.

If potential adversaries know that Bangladesh has strong military relationships with several capable states, the strategic calculation becomes more complicated.

That is precisely what deterrence is supposed to achieve.

7. Deterrence against India does not mean hostility towards India

This is an important distinction which is often lost in South Asian discussions.

Bangladesh can maintain constructive relations with India while simultaneously ensuring that its armed forces are capable of deterring Indian coercion.

There is nothing contradictory about that.

India itself maintains extensive defence capabilities precisely because it does not want to depend on the goodwill of other states for its security.

Bangladesh should have the same sovereign right.

A stronger Bangladeshi deterrent could actually make bilateral relations more stable. If both sides understand the consequences of escalation, there is less room for dangerous miscalculation.

8. The same logic applies to Myanmar

Myanmar should not disappear from this discussion simply because India receives most of the attention.

Bangladesh shares a land border with Myanmar and has already experienced the consequences of instability there.

The security situation along the south-eastern frontier can deteriorate quickly.

Bangladesh therefore needs sufficient military capability and external diplomatic support to ensure that instability in Myanmar does not translate into a crisis on Bangladeshi territory.

A wider security network can help provide that strategic depth.

9. India cannot be given a veto over Bangladesh's defence policy

Danilowicz is right that Dhaka must consider the consequences of joining the pact for relations with New Delhi.

But there is a line between taking India's reaction seriously and allowing India to determine Bangladesh's foreign policy.

Bangladesh First cannot mean:

“What will India think?”

It has to mean:

“What is in Bangladesh's national interest?”

If joining the pact strengthens Bangladesh's security, then the fact that New Delhi may dislike the decision cannot, by itself, be a sufficient reason for rejecting it.

Bangladesh should maintain good relations with India. It should also maintain good relations with China, Pakistan, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, the United States, Japan and others.

That is strategic diversification.

10. The treaty obligations must, of course, be examined carefully

There is one area where I strongly agree with Danilowicz.

Bangladesh should not sign anything without knowing precisely what it is signing.

Dhaka needs clarity on the military obligations, including what constitutes an attack, how a collective response is triggered, what forces Bangladesh could be expected to deploy and whether any deployment would remain subject to national political authorisation.

The same applies to intelligence-sharing, command arrangements, logistics, exercises and financial commitments.

These issues need to be negotiated in detail.

But they are reasons to negotiate hard, not reasons to walk away.

11. Bangladesh should demand meaningful burden-sharing

The four countries do not have equal economic or military capabilities.

There should therefore be no expectation that Bangladesh contributes in exactly the same way as Saudi Arabia or Türkiye.

Bangladesh can bring manpower, professional military personnel, peacekeeping experience, naval and air capabilities and specialised units.

Other members can contribute finance, technology, equipment, training and infrastructure.

That would be a much more sensible model.

12. The alliance could support Bangladesh's military modernisation

This may ultimately prove to be one of the most important benefits.

A serious collective-defence arrangement would require Bangladesh to improve:

secure communications;
battlefield data links;
intelligence-sharing;
joint command and control;
logistics;
air-defence integration;
naval cooperation;
special operations capabilities;
joint exercises; and
professional military education.

Those are capabilities Bangladesh needs anyway.

If an alliance accelerates their development, that is a significant strategic benefit.

13. Bangladesh should be building strategic depth, not strategic dependence

I would not advocate replacing dependence on one power with dependence on another.

That would simply be changing the problem.

Bangladesh should instead develop multiple strong defence and strategic relationships.

India should remain an important neighbour.

China remains an important defence and economic partner.

The United States remains an important global power.

Japan remains an important economic and strategic partner.

And there is no reason Bangladesh cannot simultaneously deepen defence relations with Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia.

A diversified network gives Dhaka greater freedom of manoeuvre.

14. The biggest danger is actually strategic isolation

For a country of Bangladesh's size, strategic isolation is a far greater concern than having too many defence relationships.

If Bangladesh has no meaningful security partnerships, a much larger neighbour can potentially assume that Dhaka has limited options in a crisis.

That is precisely the situation Bangladesh should avoid.

A credible network of partners raises the diplomatic and military cost of coercion.

Again, this is not about preparing for war.

It is about making sure that war remains the least attractive option for everyone.

15. Bangladesh First should be measured by outcomes

Ultimately, I think this is the real test for the BNP government.

“Bangladesh First” should not mean automatically siding with Pakistan, Saudi Arabia or Türkiye.

Nor should it mean maintaining the status quo simply because a neighbour might object to a particular decision.

It should mean examining every strategic choice according to one criterion:

Does this make Bangladesh safer, stronger and more independent?

If the answer is yes, then Bangladesh should pursue it.

If the answer is no, Dhaka should walk away.

That is the standard by which the Mecca Pact should be judged.

My assessment

I therefore believe Bangladesh should seriously explore membership rather than approach the idea primarily through the lens of what India might think.

The interoperability issue is manageable. Bangladesh already operates a diverse inventory and has extensive multinational military experience. There is particularly significant commonality with Pakistan, while Türkiye and Saudi Arabia bring capabilities and resources that could complement Bangladesh's own strengths.

The more important strategic consideration is deterrence.

Bangladesh needs to make sure that neither India nor Myanmar ever miscalculates its vulnerability, assumes that Dhaka is isolated, or believes that coercion against Bangladesh can be undertaken without serious consequences.

That is not an offensive doctrine.

It is a defensive one.

A stronger Bangladesh, with capable armed forces and a broad network of strategic partnerships, is ultimately in a better position to maintain peace with its neighbours.

For me, Bangladesh First means strategic autonomy — not strategic isolation.

Dhaka should neither become India's client nor anyone else's.

It should have enough military capability, enough diplomatic relationships and enough strategic depth that Bangladesh can make its own decisions.

If the Mecca Pact can help achieve that while preserving Bangladesh's sovereign control over the employment of its armed forces, then it deserves very serious consideration.

- Khaled Ahmed #BDMilitary

With the digital ink on the MOU barely dry, Al Jazeera asked whether the U.S. was “really preparing to drop Israel.” That alarm faded, only for the Washington Post to report a widening rift, and commentators in Washington spoke of a “moment of truth” for the president on his Israeli counterpart after Netanyahu rejected Trump’s 15-point plan in Gaza. Last year, Shlomo Ben-Ami, a former Israeli foreign minister, declared that Trump had already dumped Netanyahu. And yet every time the relationship has come down to the wire, Trump has chosen Israel. In the confrontation with Turkey, he appears to be doing so again.

Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Turkey, has for some time shown the symptoms of clientitis, the occupational affliction of ambassadors and consuls whose manifestations include adopting the host country’s perspective, taking up its case against its rivals, and drifting from their own government’s policy on its behalf.

In an interview with Mario Nawfal last week, Barrack claimed Israel “still” occupies the Golan Heights, contradicting the Trump administration’s stated position. He later withdrew the remark, but it fit a larger pattern that worries Jerusalem. He has pushed for Turkey’s readmission to the F-35 program, been notably ambivalent about Turkish military encroachment in Syria, and lobbied for Syrian sanctions relief that quashed the budding normalization talks between Syria and Israel. “He is not necessarily against Israel; he simply does not see it through Israeli eyes,” as one security source put it. Netanyahu’s own objection, according to those sources, runs deeper: He believes “Barrack is behind Trump’s support for Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa,” and connects him to Erdogan.

After last week’s confrontation over the planned deployment of Turkish forces at a Syrian airfield, the matter seems to be coming to a head.

According to Laura Loomer, Barrack has been summoned back to Washington this week for “consultations,” which she glossed, in State Department lingo, as the term for having your “ass handed to you.” She claims the mood at Foggy Bottom has curdled to the point of wanting him gone. Türkiye Today reads it very differently. When Israeli objections have run up against “Trump’s and his man’s own read of Türkiye and Syria,” the paper argues, “the president has sided with his envoy.” In its telling, the White House sees the Barrack-Israel clash as a tactical dispute rather than a strategic rupture, and is backing Barrack to keep Israel’s moves from derailing Washington’s broader stabilization plan.

If I had a nickel for every time an adversary framed Israel as the barrier to regional prosperity, only for the U.S. to eventually see through the false promise, I wouldn’t have to write this newsletter. That isn’t to say, as Tucker Carlson inevitably will, that an Israel conspiracy runs American foreign policy. It’s that, as his friend JD Vance has put it, the two countries have “many shared interests” which include: a weakened Iran, an alliance of moderate Arab states anchored to Washington and its strongest regional partner in Israel, and a Turkey whose neo-Ottoman ambitions are contained rather than indulged.

Because for all its NATO membership, Turkey is an authoritarian state with a dismal human rights record that hosts Hamas’s political leadership and bankrolls Syrian factions grown from al-Qaeda’s roots, al-Sharaa’s own included. It is antagonistic enough toward Israel that, by Trump’s own account, Erdogan was “a prime candidate” to enter the Iran war on the Iranian side, staying out only when Trump asked. It occupies northern Cyprus in defiance of international law, tests the alliance it belongs to by fielding Russian S-400s, and stonewalls the entry of countries to the alliance on Russia’s behalf.

A strong Turkey is a counterweight to American influence in the region, not a multiplier of it. It is worth remembering that when Riyadh went looking to hedge its bets against Washington, the bloc it ended up in, the Mecca pact sealed this month, put Turkey at its center.

Who knows: Maybe this time Türkiye Today has it correct; perhaps when it comes to Barrack, Trump will opt against Israel. What I do know is that every previous time we seemed to reach this crossroads, he took the path more traveled, the one that leads to Israel, even if he wandered down a few detours along the way.

📍 Dhaka, Bangladesh

⭕️ DEVELOPING — Mecca Pact Expansion Begins to Take Shape as Bangladesh Considers Joining

The Saudi–Turkey–Pakistan Mecca Joint Defence Agreement may be moving toward its first expansion.

Bangladesh’s junior foreign minister, Humayun Kabir, says Dhaka is viewing participation in the new mutual-defense pact positively and confirmed that Bangladesh’s leadership has been invited to participate.

Reuters separately reports, citing a Bangladesh Foreign Ministry source, that Saudi Arabia extended the invitation.

Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have not yet publicly confirmed it.

But this is significant.

Turkey made clear from the beginning that the three-nation agreement was designed to be expandable. Bangladesh is now the clearest concrete indication that expansion may actually be beginning.

Why Bangladesh Matters

Bangladesh is not simply another Middle Eastern state.

The overwhelmingly Sunni Muslim country has historically pursued a nonaligned foreign policy while balancing relationships with the United States, China, India and the Muslim world.

It also has no diplomatic relations with Israel and has traditionally maintained a strongly pro-Palestinian position — making it politically more compatible with the emerging bloc than many potential members.

At the same time, joining creates complications.

Bangladesh depends heavily on Western export markets, maintains important economic and security ties with Washington, and has substantial military ties with China. Dhaka is also currently moving toward negotiations for Chinese J-10CE fighter aircraft.

Its deteriorating relationship with neighboring India adds yet another dimension.

📌 BOTTOM LINE:

The Mecca Pact is beginning to look less like a one-off defense agreement between three countries and more like the potential nucleus of a larger Muslim security architecture.

Bangladesh would be an important first expansion because it extends the pact beyond the Middle East and its original three powers into South Asia.

Iran, however, remains outside.

Tehran continues to say it has received no formal invitation, despite discussions about broader regional collective security. Pakistan’s talks in Tehran reportedly produced progress toward de-escalation, reopening the Strait of Hormuz and reducing regional tensions — but no Iranian accession to the pact has been announced.

The question now is no longer simply what Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan created in Mecca.

It is how many countries they intend to bring into it — and what this alliance ultimately intends to become.

No confirmed leak. No sourced record. No smoking gun.

The talks may have failed for ordinary reasons—Iranian security concerns, Hormuz disputes, competing mediators, or irreconcilable positions. That explanation needs no spy.

But history establishes something that cannot simply be dismissed:

Egypt has repeatedly maintained access to opposing camps while simultaneously pursuing its own strategic objectives.

Iran invited to the Mecca Pact: What does it mean?

Iran confirmed it was invited to join the Mecca Pact, the defensive military alliance between Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan. 

Although no word has been said by the 3 founding members, the secrecy is strategic. Officially confirming Iran’s entry before the terms regarding militias are negotiated would trigger immediate, harsh diplomatic retaliation from Israel and the United States.

This invitation directly involves what I addressed yesterday: who pays the bill for peace in the Gulf, and how. In geopolitical conflicts, imposing military agreements usually serve as a facade to solve urgent economic and logistical bottlenecks. 

The inclusion or rapprochement of Iran in the Mecca Pact is, fundamentally, a diplomatic gambit to end Tehran’s economic suffocation and secure the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, within that regional economic arrangement I mentioned yesterday.

Saudi Arabia and its neighbors saw their ports and refineries become targets, and their economies faltered under the blockade of the strait. 

They need to reopen the maritime route at all costs to salvage their development plans, but such a move is impossible without looking like a military victory for Trump. Amidst all this, Iran signaled it accepts negotiating the management of the Strait of Hormuz and easing the blockade.

The invitation to the pact operates as a bargaining chip and a security guarantee that Arab neighbors will not support attacks on Iranian soil if the route is cleared. 

But more than that, by accepting dialogue or entering the Mecca Pact, Iran shatters the US and Israeli strategy of complete isolation. Sitting at the table with Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan grants Tehran the status of a legitimate and indispensable political actor for stability.

For the GCC, financing the neighbor’s reconstruction is not an act of charity, but a security strategy. It must be consolidated within a regional bloc that also encompasses defense aspects.
Significant progress has already been made. 

The sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Kuwait would inject billions into the Iranian economy, but the disbursements would be tied to the gradual dismantling of armed militia financing, and this remains a hurdle.

What Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan are offering Iran is a political space for Tehran to control its militias without looking like it surrendered to the West.

text:
The Frantic
Scramble To Fill the Asian Power Vacuum Left By the Fading Empire

From the Persian Gulf to the Sea of Japan, the scramble is visible in real time. The American empire, stretched past its breaking point by the Iran war, is leaving a structural vacuum. Regional powers are filling it on their own terms—quickly, pragmatically, and without waiting for Washington’s permission.
West Asia: The Mecca Pact and the Ruined Fifth Fleet
On 7 August 2026 in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed a joint defense agreement. An armed attack on one is to be treated as an attack on all. Saudi financial and energy weight, Turkish defense industry and NATO experience, and Pakistani conventional forces plus nuclear capability are now formally linked. The pact is open to expansion and is deliberately framed as complementary to existing relationships rather than a pure rejection of them. Yet its existence is the clearest admission yet that the old American security umbrella can no longer be treated as reliable.
This is not abstract. The U.S. Fifth Fleet’s headquarters at Naval Support Activity Bahrain took repeated Iranian missile and drone strikes beginning 28 February 2026. The command headquarters was rendered unusable. Multiple buildings, warehouses, barracks, a dining facility, and two satellite communications terminals were destroyed or heavily damaged. Reconstruction estimates for the base alone run into the hundreds of millions of dollars. Most personnel were evacuated; a residual staff remains. The nerve center of American naval power in the region has been structurally degraded.
The empire’s ability to project force through carrier strike groups has been exposed at the same time. Carriers have been pulled from the Western Pacific to sustain operations against Iran, creating temporary zero-carrier periods in the theater Washington still insists is the decisive one. The “laundry fire” and other incidents that forced the Gerald R. Ford off the line earlier in the conflict simply confirmed what the Houthis had already demonstrated and what peer or near-peer opponents have long understood: the carrier is a high-value, increasingly vulnerable platform against determined missile and drone saturation.
I wrote about this shift in March:
“The 500-Year Western Colonization of the World Is Over.
Gunboat diplomacy — from caravels to Carrier Strike Groups — has reached its end. The carrier has been exposed as a wobbly-kneed dinosaur.
How will any nation now project colonial force in the post-USS Ford world?”
The Mecca Pact is one answer. Regional actors are building their own collective deterrence rather than waiting for a restoration of the old order that no longer exists in practice.
East Asia: Remilitarization, Radical Korea Moves, and Dual Fronts
The eastern end of the continuum is moving even faster.
Japan under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is executing the most rapid postwar expansion of defense capabilities in decades. Spending is being accelerated toward (and beyond) the 2 percent of GDP target. Tomahawk missiles are arriving. The Ryukyu chain is being turned into a hardened missile, sensor, and directed-energy barrier. Arms-export restrictions have been relaxed. The political language of “existential threat” regarding a Taiwan contingency is now mainstream. Beijing and Moscow both denounce this as neo-militarism; Tokyo treats it as survival. The older analysis of Japan moving toward an independent force de frappe—plutonium stocks, advanced rocketry, quiet submarines, and political will—looks less speculative by the month.

Iran To Join ‘Islamic NATO’? A Geopolitical Shock Could Be Brewing

A stunning new claim from Tehran has put the Middle East’s emerging security architecture under the spotlight.

Iran has reportedly been invited to join the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, the security pact signed by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan on August 7. 

The claim was made by Mehdi Rahimi, head of Iran’s parliament-linked Khaneh Mellat news agency, who told Al Mayadeen that Tehran had received an invitation and that the proposal is “under consideration.”

The Makkah pact states that an armed attack on any one of its three members would be regarded as an attack on all, drawing comparisons with NATO’s collective-defence principle. The agreement also seeks to expand military and security cooperation among Riyadh, Ankara and Islamabad.

But there is a crucial caveat: Iran’s reported invitation has NOT been officially confirmed by Tehran’s Foreign Ministry or senior leadership. Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye have also not publicly confirmed that an invitation was extended.

If Iran ultimately joins, the consequences could be extraordinary. A framework involving Saudi Arabia and Iran—long-time regional rivals—alongside NATO member Türkiye and nuclear-armed Pakistan could fundamentally alter the balance of power across West Asia.

Iran has long advocated a regional security structure without dependence on outside powers, and Rahimi described the reported move towards a regional security umbrella as a “victory” for Tehran.

The timing is equally significant: Pakistan’s army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir is scheduled to visit Tehran on Monday, with regional security and the Iran-US crisis among the issues expected to feature in talks.

If this invitation is confirmed, the so-called ‘Islamic NATO’ could be heading for a dramatic transformation.

---

A stunning opinion piece in the right-wing Israeli newspaper *Israel Hayom* has revealed that Israeli strategic planners have concluded they can strike Turkish forces in Syria **without triggering NATO's Article 5** collective defense clause.

The article, written by Shay Gal — founder and head of Line of State, a strategic planning firm specializing in high-risk environments — argues that Turkey's NATO membership **does not automatically protect its troops operating outside Turkish territory**.

> *"The treaty protects Turkish territory; Turkish troops do not carry that territory with them onto Syrian or occupied Cypriot soil."*

## 🕋 THE MECCA PACT — THE ELEMENT ISRAEL FORGOT

On **August 7, 2026**, just two weeks before Israel's strike on Abu al-Duhur, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed the **Mecca Joint Defence Agreement**.

Israel's **August 18 strike** on Syria's Abu al-Duhur air base — located roughly **70 kilometers from the Turkish border** — was a warning shot.

Israel struck **before Turkish troops arrived** — destroying runways and military facilities rather than risking Turkish casualties.

The operational doctrine, according to Gal, is **"deny infrastructure before the flag lands"** — because once Turkish troops are present, strikes risk:
- Turkish casualties
- Turkish retaliation
- American intervention
- **Confrontation with a NATO member**
- **AND now, activation of the Mecca Pact**

Israel's strategy was built on a single assumption: **Turkey stands alone**.

The Mecca Pact shatters that assumption.

If Israel strikes Turkish forces in Syria, it is not just attacking a NATO member — it is attacking **a signatory of a mutual defense pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan**.

- **Saudi Arabia** has the money and the diplomatic weight.
- **Pakistan** has the nuclear deterrent.
- **Turkey** has the military and the strategic position.

**Together, they form a bloc that can challenge Israel's regional dominance**.

---

## ⚠️ THE WASHINGTON FACTOR — AND THE ABRAHAM ACCORDS

The Mecca Pact is not just a defense agreement. It is a **direct challenge to the US-led Abraham Accords**.

On **July 24, 2026**, Donald Trump explicitly conditioned US civilian nuclear cooperation with Saudi Arabia on Riyadh normalizing relations with Israel.

**Two weeks later, Mohammed bin Salman signed a security guarantee with Turkey and Pakistan — not with Israel**.

The message from Riyadh is clear: **Saudi Arabia will not be pressured into recognizing Israel on American terms**.

---

Israel has studied Article 5. It has concluded that NATO does not protect Turkish troops in Syria.

**But has Israel studied the Mecca Pact?**

**What happens when an attack on Turkey triggers a response from Saudi Arabia and Pakistan?**

**What happens when the world's only Muslim nuclear power is drawn into the conflict?**

Coming immediately after Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, the attack became a dangerous early test of Turkish deterrence and the emerging regional security architecture created by the pact, as Ankara moves to strengthen Syria’s new state institutions while the UAE-Israel axis faces the emergence of a security center outside Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv’s orbit.

Most dangerously, according to the information reviewed by the investigation, Israel did not use its existing military hotline with Turkey to provide advance notification of the strike. US envoy Tom Barrack acknowledged that Turkish forces did not know where the Israeli aircraft were heading or what their mission was, warning that the incident carried a genuine risk of rapidly escalating into direct confrontation between Turkey, Israel and Syria. Turkish radar capabilities were meanwhile monitoring Israeli aerial activity, creating an environment in which a miscalculation, interception or Turkish decision to scramble aircraft could have turned the raid into a direct interstate military clash.

Israel justified the operation by claiming Syria was close to allowing Turkish forces to deploy at the airbase. Syrian officials, however, said there was no Turkish military deployment at Abu al-Duhur and that a Turkish technical team had instead been assigned to repair the runway and control tower. The dispute therefore exposes a much larger struggle over Syria’s future: Ankara wants to help rebuild a capable Syrian military, while Israel is determined to preserve its ability to strike Syrian military infrastructure whenever it believes its security interests are threatened.

For Dark Box, the timing places the Mecca agreement before an extraordinarily early political and strategic test. Ankara insiders cited in the underlying reporting believe Israel was signaling that the new Saudi-Turkish-Pakistani framework would not restrict Israeli freedom of action and that Tel Aviv would continue striking where and when it chooses. The message becomes even more significant ahead of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s planned visit to Damascus, a trip that would symbolically consolidate Turkey’s growing position in post-Assad Syria.

Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv have developed extensive military, intelligence and technological cooperation, but they now face the possibility of a parallel regional structure combining Saudi political and financial weight, Turkey’s military power and expanding defense industry, and Pakistan’s large armed forces and nuclear capability. Testing Turkish deterrence—and determining whether Riyadh and Islamabad are prepared to stand behind Ankara—therefore carries strategic significance well beyond Syria.

Dark Box, however, draws an important evidentiary line: the available information supports the assessment that the Israeli attack objectively tested Turkish deterrence and came at an extraordinarily sensitive moment for the Mecca pact, but it does notprovide direct evidence that the UAE ordered, requested or operationally coordinated the Abu al-Duhur strikes. What can be established is that weakening the credibility of the emerging Mecca framework would objectively benefit actors concerned by its rise.

Anfang August haben Saudi-Arabien, die Türkei und Pakistan den Mecca Pact geschlossen. Syrien und Ägypten denken darüber nach ebenfalls beizutreten. Welche Länder kämen noch für einen Beitritt in Frage? Was könnte daraus insgesamt werden? Eine ganze Reihe von Beobachtern gehen davon aus, dass das die Retourkutsche von MBS für Trumps öffentliche Beleidigungen. Ist das so? Wie wirkt sich das alles auf mögliche Normalisierungsabkommen mit Israel aus?

---------

Der im August 2026 geschlossene Mekka-Pakt (Mecca Joint Defense Agreement) zwischen Saudi-Arabien, der Türkei und Pakistan markiert eine Zäsur in der Sicherheitsarchitektur des Nahen Ostens und Südasiens. Durch die Ausgestaltung einer kollektiven Beistandsklausel nach dem Vorbild von NATO-Artikel 5 („Ein Angriff auf einen ist ein Angriff auf alle“) bündeln drei entscheidende Mächte ihre komplementären Stärken: saudisches Kapital, türkische Rüstungstechnologie sowie die militärische Mannstärke und Nuklearmacht Pakistans.

Mögliche Beitrittskandidaten und das Potenzial des Bündnisses

Neben Syrien und Ägypten kommen primär weitere sunnitisch geprägte oder strategisch eng an das Trio gebundene Staaten für eine Erweiterung oder Kooperation infrage:

• Ägypten und Syrien: Ägypten verhandelt bereits über den Beitritt, zögert jedoch aufgrund von Bedenken wegen diplomatischer Verpflichtungen gegenüber Griechenland und Zypern sowie der Sorge vor automatischen Beistandspflichten. Das syrische Regime prüft nach Konsultationen im August 2026 ebenfalls Optionen zur Kooperation, um sich nach Jahren der Isolation abzusichern.

• Golfstaaten (z. B. Bahrain, Katar, VAE): Diese Länder sind ohnehin eng mit Saudi-Arabien vernetzt und könnten schrittweise integriert werden, um eine geschlossene Front der arabischen Halbinsel zu bilden.

• Kaspischer Raum und Zentralasien (z. B. Aserbaidschan): Aserbaidschan unterhält bereits eine enge militärische Allianz mit der Türkei und pflegt gute Beziehungen zu Pakistan und Saudi-Arabien.

• Südostasien (z. B. Bangladesch): Dhaka hat bereits öffentlich Sympathien für einen Beitritt zu wirtschaftlichen und defensiven Rahmenabkommen mit den drei Paktstaaten geäußert.

Was daraus werden könnte:

Entsteht aus dem Pakt eine voll integrierte Struktur, etabliert sich ein mächtiger sunnitischer Sicherheitsblock. Dieser könnte nicht nur als Abschreckung gegenüber Iran dienen, sondern schrittweise eigene Rüstungs- und Industriestandards setzen. Es bestünde das Potenzial für einen eigenen „Ost-NATO“-Block, der regional autark agieren kann, ohne rein von westlichen Sicherheitsgarantien abhängig zu sein.

Geopolitische Implikationen und Gesamtzusammenhänge

• Strategische Autonomie: Für Saudi-Arabien bedeutet der Pakt eine Diversifizierung seiner Sicherheitsarchitektur. Statt ausschließlich auf Washington angewiesen zu sein, holt Riad regionale Militärmächte ins Boot.

• Rüstung und Technologie: Die Türkei profitiert durch den Export von Drohnentechnologie und Kampfflugzeugen (wie dem Kaan-Programm), während Pakistan finanziell entlastet wird.

• Balance gegenüber Iran und Indien: Der Pakt wirkt als Abschreckung gegenüber regionaler Destabilisierung durch Iran, baut aber auch Druck auf Indien auf, das die militärische Annäherung zwischen Pakistan und der Türkei mit Sorge beobachtet.

Ist das die „Retourkutsche“ von MBS gegen Trump?

Analysten sehen den Schritt nicht primär als persönlichen Racheakt von Kronprinz Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) gegen US-Präsident Donald Trump, sondern als pragmatische Reaktion auf Trumps transaktionale Außenpolitik.

Trump betont seit langem das Prinzip des „Burden Sharing“ – Verbündete sollen für ihre eigene Sicherheit aufkommen und zahlen. Das saudische Königshaus hat daraus die Konsequenz gezogen, dass auf US-Beistandsgarantien im Ernstfall kein uneingeschränkter Verlass ist. Anstatt den Pakt zu verurteilen, begrüßte Trump das Abkommen öffentlich und lobte, dass die Staaten nun Eigenverantwortung für ihre Sicherheit übernehmen. MBS nutzt den Pakt somit weniger als Bestrafung, sondern als Emanzipation von unberechenbaren US-Wahlausgängen.

Auswirkungen auf Normalisierungsabkommen mit Israel

Der Mekka-Pakt verändert die Dynamik für eine potenzielle Normalisierung der Beziehungen zwischen Saudi-Arabien und Israel (Abraham-Abkommen) grundlegend:

• Erhöhte saudische Verhandlungsposition: Riad steht bei Verhandlungen mit Israel und den USA nicht mehr als Bittsteller für Schutzgarantien da. MBS kann gegenüber Israel deutlich höhere Zugeständnisse einfordern, etwa in der Palästina-Frage.

• Sorge in Israel vor einer „sunnitischen Achse“: In der israelischen Führung löst die Einbindung der Türkei – die eine sehr harte Haltung gegenüber Israel einnimmt – und des nuklear bewaffneten Pakistans Besorgnis aus. Eine militärische und technologische Bündelung dieser drei Staaten verengt den strategischen Handlungsspielraum Israels in der Region nachhaltig.

• Dämpfer für schnelle Abkommen: Eine zügige Normalisierung wird unwahrscheinlicher. Saudi-Arabien muss nun die Interessen seiner neuen Pakt-Partner – insbesondere der Türkei – berücksichtigen, was Zugeständnisse an Israel erschwert.
