text:
Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan signed a mutual defense pact in Mecca on August 7 an armed attack on one treated as an attack on all three. The comparisons to NATO started immediately. They mostly don't hold up.

The mutual-defense clause is the only real overlap. NATO runs on integrated command structures, standing military planning, and decades of joint doctrine. The Mecca pact has none of that yet  it's closer to a consultation and coordination framework than a alliance with teeth, and its own signatories have framed it that way rather than as an automatic military trigger.

The more useful way to read it: not a single alliance with one shared threat, but three states with different threats layering their security together. Saudi Arabia is focused on Iran and the Gulf. Türkiye is focused on the Levant and Israel's regional reach. Pakistan's core concern is India. That's not a weakness in the pact it's the actual logic of it. None of the three can address their own security problems alone, and none particularly wants to keep depending on Washington to do it for them.

 US attention is increasingly consumed by competition with China, and its willingness to underwrite Middle East security has looked less reliable for over a decade reinforced, in these three countries' view, by unconditional US backing for Israel through the current war. China hasn't stepped in to fill that role either. The pact isn't a rejection of American security guarantees so much as insurance against their absence.

Whether that insurance means anything depends on follow-through most frameworks like this struggle with: institutions, joint planning, actual coordination under pressure. The pact is real. Whether it becomes more than a signing ceremony is still an open bet.

text:
#Saudi_Arabia opposed #Egypt’s inclusion in #Mecca defense pact: MEE

Saudi Arabia opposed Egypt’s inclusion in the newly signed Mecca Joint Defence Agreement between Saudi Arabia, #Türkiye and #Pakistan, according to three Saudi sources familiar with the discussions who spoke anonymously to Middle East Eye (MEE).

The sources said Riyadh had grown increasingly frustrated with President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s government, questioning Egypt’s strategic value and its reliability on key regional security issues. 

The agreement was signed on 7 August in Mecca by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. It commits the three countries to regard an armed attack against any one of them as an attack against all three, although the pact leaves unclear how the commitment would be activated and what military assistance would entail.

According to the Saudi sources, Riyadh’s concerns included Egypt’s limited role in the Saudi-led war against Yemen’s Houthis and what they described as Cairo’s inadequate support during the recent US-Israeli conflict involving Iran. They also pointed to Egypt’s close ties with the United Arab Emirates, amid growing Saudi-UAE tensions over regional issues including Yemen.

The sources further questioned Egypt’s military effectiveness and reliability, while contrasting it with Türkiye’s advanced defence industry and Pakistan’s established arms production and large standing army.

Turkish sources, meanwhile, told MEE that Ankara had actively pushed for Egypt to join the pact and formally proposed its inclusion. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan later described Egypt as a “natural partner,” suggesting Cairo could join at a later stage once technical issues are resolved.

One former senior Saudi adviser close to decision-making dismissed claims that Egypt had itself rejected membership, arguing that Cairo would have welcomed the financial benefits of joining. The adviser also criticised Egypt’s longstanding reliance on Saudi, US and other external support without providing equivalent strategic returns.

Puppeteer, Puppet, and the Pact 

For India, the Mecca Pact or its mutual protection security umbrella is insignificant because the US has already offered its security guarantee for Pakistan by trying to intervene after its suspected nuclear arsenal depot at Kirana Hills were hit during India’s Op Sindoor. India does not have a land or sea border with Türkiye nor any dispute thereof. If at all India ever had a tiff with Türkiye, it was over Pakistan. After all, a NATO member is expected to be overtly friendly with an Anglo-American military asset in the West Asian theatre. Then, there is Saudi Arabia, a genuine friend of India and a vital supplier of energy with no conflict nor even mild mutual disagreements.

So, the Mecca Pact, thus leaves just Pakistan in the equation. And the US has effectively taken over Pakistan’s foreign policy formulations reducing its leadership to civilian messengers and uniformed butlers. The difference this security guarantee makes to India is huge, no doubt. India’s kinetic response doctrine against Pakistan’s proxy terror attacks obviously gets compromised once the US throws its security blanket over the rogue nation, for whatever strategic objectives. It is back to the drawing board for India to devise a new response to terror attacks. India is forced to fashion dynamic solutions in such treacherous quicksands. But the Mecca Pact is least of its worries.

The biggest fallacy about the Pact is the claim that it is an Islamic NATO. The leader of the Islamic world right now is Iran ––– the lone Muslim nation taking on the mighty US and Israel. There can never be an Islamic NATO that stands with Israel and US against Iran, which is what the Mecca Pact attempts to do. Saudi Arabia is under attack from Iran and its allies Houthis. It needs legitimacy within the Islamic Umma to bomb Iran and that is what Israel and the US are trying to provide by pushing its proxy Pakistan. Iran has targeted what it calls the Arab dynastic allies of the US for providing military bases to launch attacks to seize the third largest oil reserves of the world. So, the only way Saudi Arabia can retaliate without antagonising the entire Muslim world is by threatening to invoke the mutual protection clause of the conveniently nicknamed “Muslim NATO.”

Now, this new NATO does not wash because the US’ Arab allies have been waiting to sign the Abraham Accords with Israel and the only hitch so far has been latter’s genocidal war in Gaza. Had Israel and the US conquered Iran in a fortnight as initially they had planned, everything would have fallen in place. But no longer. As the Iran conflict drags on with no end in sight and the American war machine showing signs of ageing, the US is desperate for more religious Islamic optics in West Asia. And India has nothing to worry so long as the conflict continues because sooner than later the favourite butler would have to send his men to die for the empire, for which his nation was created.

🇸🇦🇹🇷🇵🇰 THE MIDDLE EAST AFTER AMERICA?

For five decades, Washington sat at the center of the Middle East's security architecture. The Mecca Agreement may be the clearest sign yet that this era is coming to an end.
@CFR_org 's Steven Cook argues that the new Saudi-Turkish-Pakistani defense pact isn't simply another regional alliance. It reflects a deeper shift: regional powers are beginning to build their own security order rather than relying on the United States to organize it.

On August 7, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement. Reporting indicates it contains something resembling NATO's Article 5: an attack against one would be treated as an attack against all.

Taken literally, the implications are extraordinary.

A future India-Pakistan war could theoretically create obligations for Saudi Arabia and Turkey. A Turkish confrontation with Israel could raise questions for Riyadh and Islamabad. And Saudi Arabia now has a formal security structure outside the American architecture that protected the Gulf for decades.

Yet Cook argues the military guarantee itself isn't really the most important part.

Indeed, when the Houthis attacked Saudi Arabia shortly after the agreement was signed - including the strike on the Aramco refinery at Jizan - Riyadh did not summon Turkish or Pakistani forces.

The significance lies somewhere deeper: Saudi Arabia is no longer relying exclusively on Washington to organize its security environment.

For roughly half a century, the United States was the hub connecting much of the Middle East's security architecture - Saudi Arabia, the Gulf monarchies, Egypt, Jordan, Turkey and, increasingly, Israel.

Meca suggests regional powers are beginning to construct an architecture in which they themselves become the organizing nodes. And that could produce something the Middle East has not really had during the era of American primacy: competing security blocs.

The emerging fault line is fascinating.

On one side is the architecture Washington has spent years trying to build around the Abraham Accords: Israel integrated economically and strategically with Arab states, eventually connected through projects such as the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor.

On the other may now be an alternative centered on Saudi Arabia + Turkey + Pakistan.

And the competition isn't limited to military alliances. Cook points to proposals by Riyadh and Ankara to reroute the IMEC rail corridor itself.

Instead of Saudi Arabia → Jordan → Israel → Mediterranean → Europe, the alternative would effectively become: Saudi Arabia → Jordan → Syria → Turkey → Europe. Israel would be bypassed entirely.

That makes something @jaredkushner wrote today particularly interesting. Marking six years since the Abraham Accords, Kushner argued that the Middle East is again at an “inflection point” and called for “an even broader movement around cooperation, shared prosperity and security.”

Hours later, @axios reported that Kushner plans to return to Israel next week as Washington tries to advance Trump's Gaza framework and potentially hold broader regional talks.

So two competing visions are now becoming visible at almost exactly the same moment.

Washington's vision: expand the Abraham Accords and integrate Israel deeper into a regional economic and security system.

The emerging alternative: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan constructing their own security framework - potentially accompanied by trade corridors that bypass Israel altogether.

Cook's conclusion is deliberately provocative: after five decades, he argues, “it is no longer possible to talk about a U.S.-led order in the Middle East.”

Whether that obituary proves premature remains to be seen. The U.S. still possesses military capabilities and regional relationships none of these states can individually replace.

But the structural change is harder to dismiss: Middle Eastern powers are now shaping the regional order themselves.

The Makkah Pact: Three Powers, No Common Enemy
Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan signed a collective-defence agreement in Makkah on 7 August. Its formula is deliberately forceful: an armed attack against one will be considered an attack against all. Yet the treaty’s operational provisions remain unpublished, while the signatories face different enemies, retain consequential ties with Washington and pursue economic interests that often pull in opposite directions. The pact may still reshape security from the Red Sea to South Asia—not by becoming a “Muslim NATO”, but by connecting Saudi capital, Turkish military industry and Pakistani strategic power.

A guarantee without a doctrine
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Pakistani Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement on 7 August 2026. According to the official joint statement published by Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry, the accord is intended to strengthen collective deterrence and expand “all aspects” of defence cooperation.

Islamabad subsequently defined it as a defensive agreement, directed against no state and consistent with the right of collective self-defence recognized by Article 51 of the United Nations Charter. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar presented it as an instrument for protecting sovereignty, territorial integrity and national populations, not as a mechanism of confrontation. The language is categorical; the obligations behind it are not yet public.

The complete treaty, its annexes and any national reservations have not been released. The available documents do not identify a permanent council, an integrated headquarters, assigned forces, an activation deadline or a common definition of “armed attack”. They do not clarify whether the guarantee covers cyber operations, proxy attacks, ships outside national waters, overseas bases or critical infrastructure operated by private companies. Nor do they establish that military force would follow automatically.

That distinction separates a political guarantee from an operational alliance. NATO’s Article 5 is supported by a council, integrated planning, common standards, standing commands, exercises and logistics developed over decades. Makkah currently offers the promise; its machinery remains to be built.

Three different maps of danger
For Riyadh, the immediate threat map begins with missiles, drones, energy installations, the Gulf and the southern frontier. A strike against an oil-processing plant or Red Sea terminal can produce consequences far beyond the physical damage: lost export capacity, higher insurance premiums, disrupted shipping and a fiscal shock transmitted through global energy markets.

Türkiye reads the region differently. Ankara’s declared priorities include the PKK, its Syrian and Iranian extensions as defined by the Turkish government, instability in Syria and Iraq, and the obligations arising from NATO membership. Iran is a competitor, but also a neighbour, energy interlocutor and counterterrorism partner. On 30 January 2026, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, speaking beside Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, argued that the PKK/PJAK threatened both countries and called for joint action.

Pakistan’s principal interstate contingency remains India. The seriousness of that exposure was demonstrated in May 2025, when four days of military action ended only after the two Directors General of Military Operations agreed to stop firing and military activity on land, at sea and in the air from 17:00 on 10 May. The Indian government’s account and Pakistan’s official statement differ sharply over responsibility, but both confirm the ceasefire understanding.

Here lies the pact’s hardest contradiction. Pakistan may regard an Indian strike as the clearest possible test of collective defence. Saudi Arabia, however, maintains a Strategic Partnership Council with New Delhi. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Mohammed bin Salman co-chaired its second meeting in Jeddah on 22 April 2025; a further India–Saudi Security Working Group met in Riyadh on 28 January 2026. Türkiye also has commercial interests to protect: India’s Foreign Ministry values bilateral trade at $6.88 billion in fiscal year 2025–26.

An India–Pakistan war would therefore be more likely to produce Saudi and Turkish mediation, defensive assistance and political support than their automatic entry into combat. The solidarity clause cannot erase the economic and diplomatic relationships surrounding it.

Iran presents the inverse problem. It is a central security concern for Riyadh, especially where missiles, drones, Iraqi armed groups or Yemen’s Ansarallah are involved. For Islamabad and Ankara, it remains a state with which borders, trade and regional diplomacy must be managed. Pakistan was still presenting itself in 2026 as a facilitator between Tehran and Washington. An explicitly anti-Iranian interpretation of Makkah would compromise that role.

Israel creates stronger political convergence but equally severe escalation risks. Pakistan does not recognize Israel; Türkiye has adopted an increasingly confrontational position toward Israeli regional operations; Saudi policy remains tied to the Palestinian question, Arab diplomacy and its relationship with Washington. A direct Israeli attack on a signatory’s territory would be difficult to leave unanswered. A strike against a non-state organization operating from that territory would reopen every unresolved question about attribution, sovereignty and proportionality.

The maritime imperative
The clearest shared mission lies at sea. Unlike India or Iran, maritime insecurity does not require the three governments to agree on a permanent enemy. It requires them to protect navigation, ports, energy terminals and crews.

The International Maritime Organization’s verified record listed 60 confirmed incidents affecting Red Sea shipping between 10 January 2024 and August 2026, including 58 by the end of 2025. A further 17 incidents occurred between November 2023 and 9 January 2024. Security Council Resolution 2812, adopted on 14 January 2026, extended the UN reporting mandate for Houthi attacks on merchant and commercial vessels.

Hormuz has produced an even wider emergency. As of 11 August 2026, the IMO estimated that more than 20,000 seafarers, together with port and offshore workers, had been affected by regional instability. Its evacuation framework moved 136 vessels out of the Gulf between 23 and 26 June—14 on the first day, 41 on the second, 51 on the third and 30 on the fourth—evacuating an estimated 2,900 seafarers.

These are operational facts around which a credible pact can be constructed. Saudi Arabia provides geography, ports and financing; Pakistan brings access to the Arabian Sea and established naval experience; Türkiye contributes naval platforms, unmanned systems, electronics and command capabilities. The first meaningful institutions may consequently be a maritime information-fusion centre, coordinated escort procedures, port counter-drone defences and common protocols for search and rescue, piracy and mine warfare.

Precedents already exist. The Royal Saudi Naval Forces and Pakistan Navy conducted Naseem Al Bahr 15 in the Arabian Sea, while the Royal Saudi Air Force participated in Anatolian Phoenix 2025 at Konya. These bilateral connections could be assembled into a trilateral exercise cycle more quickly than a unified land command.

Washington remains inside the room

The same package included civil-nuclear, critical-minerals and artificial-intelligence agreements.

Three days later, Pakistan signed the Makkah accord.

None of the signatories has an economic interest in forcing a binary choice between Makkah and Washington.

But in a prolonged conflict with India, one question becomes critical: how does Pakistan keep foreign weapons flowing into the country?

Pakistan depends heavily on maritime trade, while Saudi Arabia and Türkiye are separated from Pakistan by long supply routes.

Moving large volumes of ammunition, spares and military equipment during an active war is far harder than promising support on paper.

That geography works in India’s favour. 

The Indian Navy’s expanding maritime surveillance and long-range strike capability gives India ability to put pressure on Pakistan’s external military logistics.

India does not need to stop every shipment. Making the supply line slow, risky and unpredictable could itself put serious pressure on Pakistan during a prolonged war.

India also has deep economic and strategic ties with Saudi Arabia, giving New Delhi another channel to make its concerns clear to Riyadh.

the Mecca Pact may expand Pakistan’s list of supporters, but India still has the geography, naval reach and diplomatic leverage to make sustained wartime resupply far harder.

Far from heralding the birth of a “Sunni Nato” directed against Iran, the emerging Mecca pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan may reveal a far more consequential geopolitical shift: Riyadh’s waning confidence in American protection and the gradual fragmentation of the US-led security order that has shaped the Middle East for more than seven decades.

“Three of the most important Sunni Muslim states, alarmed by Iran's strategic ascendancy and the turmoil engulfing the region, were finally banding together, the argument went, to establish a military alliance that could eventually become a "Sunni" Islamic version of Nato…

Yet the Nato analogy obscures a more fundamental question: after more than seven decades of overwhelming American military predominance in the Middle East, why does Saudi Arabia believe it needs Turkey and Pakistan to help guarantee its security?

The Mecca Agreement could prove to be less about constructing a new alliance against Iran than about the gradual unravelling of the American-centred security order that has dominated the region since the end of the Second World War”

✍️ Opinion by Sami al-Arian

The Alliance China Did Not Join

How Chinese military power can travel without Chinese guarantees

Part I of a two-part series on the Mecca Pact and the changing geometry of Middle Eastern security

On August 7th Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed a defence pact in Mecca with a provision that invited an obvious comparison: an armed attack on one would be treated as an attack on all. The resemblance to NATO’s Article 5 was hard to miss, even if the obligations behind that promise remain much less precisely defined.

The explanations were equally familiar. The pact has been described as a Sunni NATO, a hedge against Iran and Israel, and an insurance policy against the declining predictability of American protection. Each captures part of the story. None quite explains one of its more consequential features.

China did not join it.

No Chinese leader stood in Mecca. Beijing made no defence commitment. Yet Chinese military technology is already embedded in one of the pact’s most capable armed forces—and through that force has begun to acquire relevance elsewhere in the region.

Pakistan is the conduit. China supplied 80% of its major arms imports in 2021-25, up from 73% in the previous five-year period. The relationship has long since moved beyond the simple transfer of finished weapons. Chinese aircraft, air-defence systems, naval platforms and associated technologies have been absorbed into Pakistan’s own military capacity.

This year showed why that distinction matters.

During the Iran war Pakistan deployed roughly 8,000 troops to Saudi Arabia, together with JF-17 fighters, drones and a Chinese-made HQ-9 air-defence system. The deployment was financed by Saudi Arabia and remained under Pakistani operational control.

China did not defend Saudi Arabia. Pakistan did.

But part of what Pakistan deployed had been built through the Chinese defence-industrial system.

Military technology travels twice.

Arms statistics capture the first journey, when a weapon moves from supplier to buyer. They are less good at capturing the second. Once foreign technology has been absorbed into another country’s armed forces, it becomes part of a sovereign military capability that can be trained with, deployed or used to provide security elsewhere.

A Chinese system sold to Pakistan does not remain merely a Chinese export. In Pakistani hands it becomes part of Pakistan’s own ability to project military power.

That creates a pathway of influence that conventional measures of Chinese military reach tend to miss.

Beijing did not order the Saudi deployment. It did not command Pakistani forces and offered no guarantee to defend Saudi territory. What China acquired was something subtler: security relevance at one remove.

The Mecca Pact could widen the significance of that mechanism.

Saudi Arabia is already the clearest case. Riyadh remains deeply embedded in the American military system, and there is no serious evidence that Pakistani or Chinese-derived capabilities are replacing it. The important development is additive. American high-end systems can coexist with Pakistani manpower, Turkish defence technology and Chinese-origin platforms operated by another sovereign military.

This is redundancy rather than realignment.

But a three-way defence commitment means Pakistan’s military value no longer matters only to Saudi Arabia.

Turkey offers a less immediate but potentially important example.

Ankara remains protected by NATO, and nothing in the Mecca Pact approaches the military depth of the Atlantic alliance. Yet Article 5 is not an automatic order for every ally to enter a war in the same way. The problem becomes still more complicated if a confrontation begins outside Turkish territory—in Syria, for example—and escalates towards Turkey rather than beginning with an unambiguous attack on it.

That distinction has become less theoretical as relations between Turkey and Israel have deteriorated. The two have already had to manage competing military interests in Syria, and Israeli actions there have prompted increasingly explicit security warnings from Ankara.

A direct Turkish-Israeli war remains an extreme scenario. NATO would also remain central to Turkey’s calculations if Turkish territory itself were attacked.

But additional deterrence still has value precisely because governments cannot know in advance how a crisis will develop.

The Mecca Pact gives Ankara another militarily capable partner in Pakistan. And Pakistan enters that relationship with a force structure substantially strengthened by Chinese technology.

For Turkey, the relevant benefit is therefore not necessarily access to Chinese weapons. It is access to a partner whose ability to fight, deploy and deter has been enlarged by them.

China need not arm Turkey directly for Chinese military industry to alter Turkey’s security options.

That is what turns the Pakistani example from a bilateral curiosity into something more consequential. Once Chinese-derived capabilities enter a multilateral defence relationship through Pakistan, their strategic relevance is no longer confined to the original China-Pakistan transaction—or even to Pakistan’s deployment in Saudi Arabia.

This does not make Turkey dependent on China. Quite the opposite: Ankara has invested heavily in its own defence industry and has little interest in replacing dependence on Washington with dependence on Beijing. Political friction with China also remains, including over the Uyghur issue and competing interests across Eurasia.

But strategic autonomy does not require keeping every external system at a distance. It can also come from having enough overlapping options that no single relationship becomes exclusive.

Pakistan’s role in the pact therefore reveals something important about Chinese military power abroad. A country equipped with Chinese technology can become more valuable to third states even when those states themselves have little intention of entering China’s strategic orbit.

Iran provides an equally important limit to the argument.

China retains deep economic and political ties with Tehran even as Chinese-derived military capabilities become relevant to states worried about Iranian power. This year’s war also demonstrated that Beijing’s economic importance to Iran does not give it command over Iranian security policy.

China has therefore not secretly chosen the Mecca Pact over Iran. Nor does Chinese technology inside Pakistan turn the pact into a Chinese instrument.

The significance lies elsewhere.

For decades, assessments of Chinese military influence abroad have concentrated on three visible indicators: arms sales, overseas deployments and political alignment. Pakistan suggests that a fourth deserves greater attention.

What happens after imported military technology has been absorbed?

A recipient state does not remain merely a customer. Over time it can become a producer of security in its own right. When its forces deploy abroad or enter new defence arrangements, some of the capabilities created by the original supplier move with them.

The supplier’s strategic footprint can therefore spread without its soldiers moving, its flag appearing or a new treaty being signed.

The Mecca Pact gives this mechanism a larger stage. Pakistan is no longer merely a major recipient of Chinese military technology. It is now part of a collective-defence arrangement with two of the most consequential powers in the Middle East.

That does not give Beijing control over the arrangement. But it means the military relationship China spent decades building with Pakistan can generate consequences far beyond South Asia.

The distinction matters for Washington as well.

American military power remains much deeper in the Middle East than anything China has built there. Its bases, intelligence networks, weapons systems, logistics and capacity for sustained high-intensity warfare are not being replicated by the appearance of a few Chinese-derived systems inside a Pakistani deployment.

Yet dominance and indispensability are not quite the same thing.

The United States can remain the region’s strongest external military power while becoming less necessary to every security connection within it.

China faces the reverse possibility. It can remain unwilling to become the Middle East’s chief security guarantor while becoming increasingly difficult to bypass.

That is a different model of power.

The Mecca Pact is not a Chinese alliance.

Its significance for China begins there.

#MeccaPact

A common bureaucratic critique of this alliance is that it creates friction by crossing geographic Combatant Command (COCOM) boundaries, since Turkey sits under European Command (USEUCOM) while Saudi Arabia and Pakistan sit under CENTCOM. In the field, however, these barriers are merely paper tigers.
 
The successful transfer of Israel from EUCOM to CENTCOM proved that these operational lines are highly flexible administrative adjustments, not functional dead ends. More importantly, the foundational legal and technical plumbing required for these three nations to operate together is already hardcoded into the region's architecture. All three signatories have long-standing, active Title 22 security assistance arrangements, Communication Interoperability and Security Memorandums of Agreement (CISMOAs), and tactical data link capabilities with the United States. Furthermore, Turkey operates entirely on NATO Allied Joint Doctrine and Standardization Agreements (STANAGs). Because U.S. and NATO doctrines are identical, integrating operations during a crisis follows a highly familiar, pre-vetted playbook.
 
4. Maximizing U.S. Soft Power and Edging Out China
 
Far from losing leverage, the Mecca Pact hands the United States a massive soft-power opening through Foreign Military Sales (FMS) and security assistance. The signing of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement on August 7, 2026, by Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan has triggered predictable anxiety in Western foreign policy circles. Commentators have quickly branded this trilateral, NATO-style collective defense pact as a fracturing of the traditional, U.S.-led security order in the Middle East. They interpret it as a defiant declaration of strategic autonomy.
 
However, looking at the situation from a grand strategy perspective reveals a completely different reality. This regional security alliance does not represent a rejection of Washington. Instead, it serves as a powerful force multiplier for long-standing U.S. geopolitical objectives. By creating an organic, self-sustaining defense architecture, the Mecca Pact helps enable the long-desired American "Pacific Shift," establishes a practical framework for Israeli-Palestinian stability, and offers a prime opportunity to expand U.S. soft power while systematically squeezing out Chinese and Russian influence.
 
1. Enabling the Pacific Shift
 
For over a decade, Washington has openly declared a need to shift resources to the Indo-Pacific to counter the rise of China and the provocations of North Korea. Yet, this "pivot" has consistently been held back by the security realities of the Middle East. Confronting threats from Iranian proxies has continuously tied down high-demand, low-density U.S. military assets, such as Patriot and THAAD missile batteries, Carrier Strike Groups, and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) platforms.
 
The Mecca Pact changes this operational math by shifting the burden of routine regional deterrence from American taxpayers to local heavyweights. By combining Saudi financial resources, Turkey’s large-scale NATO-standard army, and Pakistan’s conventional manpower and nuclear deterrent, these nations are establishing a formidable collective shield. As this alliance takes over the responsibility of regional defense, the Pentagon can safely write down its permanent footprint in the Central Command (CENTCOM) area of responsibility. This allows the U.S. to confidently reallocate those high-end defense assets to the First Island Chain in Asia.
 
2. A Blueprint for Palestinian Stability and Normalization
 
Critics argue that binding Saudi Arabia’s defense to Turkey and Pakistan—two nations often critical of Israel—will permanently stall the expansion of the Abraham Accords. This is a short-sighted view. In reality, Middle East normalization hinges entirely on a viable, face-saving path to a two-state solution for the Palestinian situation, which Saudi Arabia has maintained as a strict requirement.
 
The primary obstacle to a two-state solution has always been the security vacuum. Israel will not accept a sovereign Palestinian state if it fears the territory will be taken over by hostile, destabilizing non-state actors. The Mecca Pact provides an elegant solution to this impasse:
 
•Organic Peacekeeping: The pact states can provide a highly credible, well-funded, and culturally integrated peacekeeping force to secure a transitioning Palestinian state.
•Credible Enforcement: Backed by Saudi capital, Turkish NATO-trained troops, and Pakistani counter-insurgency experience, this alliance can offer the strict security guarantees that toothless UN mandates never could.
•The Path to Normalization: By providing Israel with a tangible security partner and Palestinians with stable governance, the Mecca Pact could serve as the literal bridge to Saudi-Israeli normalization, rather than a barrier to it.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif just signed a trilateral defence deal that basically says: “You touch one of us, you get the whole squad.”  
The wording is a deliberate, almost troll-ish carbon-copy of NATO’s Article 5 — because nothing says “we’re done being polite” like borrowing the West’s own club rules and pointing them at the guy who keeps bombing everyone else’s infrastructure while screaming “existential threat!” every Tuesday.
Earlier today, three people were killed when the Houthis finally scored a direct hit on a cargo ship in the Red Sea — the first fatal one since the whole mess started. Shocking, right? Almost as if continuous Israeli airstrikes on Yemen, Gaza, Lebanon and Syria might eventually produce some pushback. Who could have predicted?
Meanwhile Turkey and Pakistan are eyeing their borders with Iran and muttering “please don’t let the chaos spill over… especially the kind that starts with a certain air force deciding ‘pre-emptive self-defence’ means turning the map into Swiss cheese.”
So is this pact a scary anti-Iran gang-up?  
Or is it just the early blueprints of a regional security club that finally noticed the elephant in the room isn’t Tehran — it’s the heavily-armed, internationally-subsidised room-mate who keeps rearranging the furniture with missiles and then demanding everyone else pay for the damages?
Either way, the biggest plot twist might not even be about Iran. It might be the moment the rest of the neighbourhood quietly decided that “never again” shouldn’t only apply to one country.

text:
Dr Chellaney, I agree with your central observation and I think you have not followed it to its conclusion.

You note that the only other acknowledged Vance call to Mr Modi came on the night of the ninth of May, and that India suspended the operation the following day. Sit with what you have just written. An American Vice President telephoned at midnight, and within twenty four hours the operation stopped. Whatever the content of that call, the sequence tells the story. The ceasefire was then announced from Washington by President Trump, not from South Block. You are correct to wonder what is urgent enough to prompt the latest call. The prior question is why Delhi’s operational decisions arrive by telephone from Ohio at all.

Now the tenth of May 2025, which your account passes over. On that day Indian television channels all of them told 1.4 billion people that Karachi port was under bombardment, that Lahore was burning, that Islamabad was under Indian control, that Pakistani corps formations had surrendered. Every word of it false. 

No correction was issued, no apology offered, no anchor removed. Fact check it against your own broadcasters’ archives. A nation that had won would not have needed any of it.

And notice where everyone ended up in 2026 #Islamabad. Pakistan mediates between Washington and Tehran. Riyadh and Ankara sign a mutual defence commitment. Where in any of those rooms is Dr Jaishankar? Where is the Prime Minister? After eighty seven foreign trips and fourteen years of describing Pakistan as the epicentre of terror, Pakistan is now treated as the region’s stabiliser and India is treated as an important market.

On the Makkah pact, you of all people should read it accurately. It is not an anti India instrument and it is not anti Iran. The Iranian foreign minister was in Islamabad while your commentators were denouncing a Sunni NATO. It is about a Muslim world that has watched Sudan, Libya, Syria and Yemen destroy themselves, that has watched Daesh and Al Qaeda grow in ungoverned space, and that has finally decided to organise a deterrent architecture rather than wait for one. 

Five hundred billion dollars of Saudi platforms that need trained crews. Turkish industry. Pakistani operational depth and integrated air defence, the capability demonstrated on the night of the sixth and seventh that nobody in Delhi wishes to discuss. Fifty seven states, a combined defence spend of over 155 billion dollars, and the free flow of oil through the Red Sea. Why would they not?

On parity, you already know the arithmetic. Ten billion against eighty five, soon ninety five, plus forty billion in Rafales. If India had established dominance, that procurement would be unnecessary. The strategic balance was not disturbed by the Makkah pact. It was disturbed by Sindoor, which combined an underestimation of Pakistan with an overestimation of Indian capability. 

That is the drawing board to return to.
On water, the position has reversed within a year. Delhi refused to convene the Indus Commission, then declared the treaty in abeyance, then filled dams to the brim last August with consequences felt in both Punjabs. Now, facing Chinese construction upstream on the Yarlung Tsangpo, India demands consultation mechanisms and data sharing. 

The principle you deny to Pakistan you invoke against Beijing. And the alarm is misplaced anyway, since most of the Brahmaputra’s flow is generated by rainfall below the Chinese stretch.

On terror, your own doctrine has become incoherent. India told the world that harbouring terrorists makes a state a target. After Pahalgam, family homes were dynamited within days, some two thousand Kashmiris were detained, Pakistan offered a neutral international inquiry and Delhi refused. Meanwhile India funds a Taliban regime sheltering roughly a hundred thousand TTP fighters who have killed seventy thousand Pakistanis, including a hundred and thirty two children at the Army Public School in Peshawar. 1/2

The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement is not just another mutual-defence clause. It marks the start of a new regional security architecture.

For decades, the Gulf-South Asia security order was built around Western guarantors. This pact signals something different: three Muslim-majority powers, Saudi Arabia’s capital, Pakistan’s nuclear deterrent, Turkey’s NATO-scale military, choosing to build their own collective deterrence, on their own terms, in their own holy city.

It’s a signal to Iran. It’s a signal to Israel. It’s a signal to Washington that “burden-sharing” cuts both ways, allies who build their own security don’t need to wait for anyone’s green light.

The Mecca Pact isn’t the ceiling. It’s the floor of something bigger.

text:
This is The DEFCON Warning System. Alert status for 1 PM UTC, Monday, 10 August 2026:

Condition Green – DEFCON 5.

There are currently no imminent nuclear threats at this time.

The Ahmad Vahidi Nuclear Quote Has No Credible Source

On 5 August, a statement attributed to IRGC commander-in-chief Ahmad Vahidi circulated online, claiming that Iran would continue working on nuclear weapons for as long as the United States and Israel possessed them. The allegation was subsequently repeated by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the United States ambassador to the United Nations, Senator Rick Scott, Fox News, and other outlets.

However, no original evidence has emerged. An investigation by the Israeli news organisation Ynet found no Iranian speech, video, transcript, news-agency report, or independent wire report containing the statement. It traced the claim through an Indian nationalist social-media account and English-language Israeli accounts before it was repeated by senior officials. An informed Iranian source quoted by the Tehran Times also denied that an Iranian military commander had made the remarks.

The available evidence therefore supports the conclusion that Vahidi did not make the statement, or, at minimum, that there is no credible basis for claiming that he did. The purported quote should not be treated as an Iranian admission of a nuclear-weapons programme.

That correction does not resolve the separate questions surrounding Iran’s enrichment activities, undeclared work, inspection access, or long-term intentions. It does show how an unsupported claim can move rapidly from social media into official political statements. In a crisis involving nuclear facilities and active warfare, such a misinformation chain can distort threat assessments and create pressure for military action.

Iran Is Betting That Time Is on Its Side

Iranian leaders increasingly believe that the United States will eventually have to accept Iranian control over the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran’s calculation rests on the war’s unpopularity in the United States, pressure from high energy prices before the November congressional elections, declining stocks of important American munitions, and the potential cost of reopening the strait by force.

An adviser to Iran’s chief negotiator characterised Iran’s objective as the enemy’s defeat rather than merely an agreement. Iran has also insisted that the strait will not return to its pre-war status as an unrestricted international waterway.

During the week, Iran and Oman reported progress on arrangements for shipping lanes through the strait. A proposal under discussion would give Iran authority over ships entering the Gulf, although important details remained unresolved and the United States has repeatedly opposed Iranian control of the waterway.

By 10 August, Iran said an agreement with Oman was nearing completion, but it made clear that this would not automatically reopen the strait. Tehran demanded an end to United States military threats and the naval blockade, the lifting of sanctions, the release of frozen assets, compensation for war damage, and an end to attacks against Iran and its regional allies. Iran and the United States continued to exchange messages through intermediaries, but they were not engaged in direct negotiations.

Why an Iranian “Victory” Could Affect the Nuclear Question

Control of the Strait of Hormuz is not, on its own, a nuclear-war issue. The nuclear danger arises if Iran concludes that sustained military and economic coercion can force the United States to accept Iranian freedom of action in other areas.

The immediate negotiations have pushed the nuclear dispute into the background. An Iran-based analyst told the Associated Press that this delay serves Tehran’s interests because control of the strait would provide leverage when nuclear negotiations eventually resume.

If Washington lifted sanctions and military pressure without securing enforceable nuclear restrictions, renewed International Atomic Energy Agency access, and an accounting of Iran’s enriched uranium, Iranian leaders could conclude that time and resistance had defeated Western non-proliferation pressure. That could allow Iran to preserve or expand enrichment capacity, restrict inspections, disperse sensitive work, or pursue weaponisation-related activity clandestinely.

This is a risk, not an established outcome. Iran’s economy remains badly damaged, its conventional forces have suffered heavily, and indirect communication continues. A settlement that first reduces military activity and then restores verifiable nuclear controls could move the strategic situation away from both conventional and nuclear escalation. The decisive question is whether the nuclear file is merely postponed or effectively abandoned.

American Munitions Pressure May Change Deterrence Calculations

There are disputed reports that the United States had used “virtually all” of its available Army Tactical Missile Systems and Precision Strike Missiles during the five-month Iran war, according to people familiar with internal data. One source said the United States had also expended slightly less than half of its global Tomahawk cruise-missile inventory. A study cited by Reuters estimated that approximately 65 per cent of Patriot interceptors had been used between February and July, while the THAAD interceptor inventory was at least 38 per cent lower than at the war’s beginning.

The White House and Pentagon disputed suggestions that the United States could not meet its military commitments, stating that sufficient capabilities remained and that production was increasing. Precise remaining quantities are not publicly available.

The reported drawdown does not weaken the United States’ strategic nuclear deterrent. It may, however, affect how Iran, Russia, China, and North Korea judge American capacity to sustain several conventional conflicts at once. A perceived shortage of long-range strike weapons and missile interceptors could encourage adversaries to probe United States commitments or prolong conflicts in the belief that time favours them.

The Makkah Pact Creates a New, but Undefined, Defence Commitment

On 7 August, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement. The official joint statement says that an armed attack against any one of the three states will be regarded as an attack against all three. It also calls for broader defence cooperation and collective deterrence.

The publicly released statement does not specify what assistance each country must provide, what actions would qualify as an armed attack, or whether a response would be automatic. Pakistan described the pact as defensive and consistent with Article 51 of the United Nations Charter. Turkey said the members would consult on the degree, form, and format of support required in a crisis.

Pakistan possesses nuclear weapons, while Turkey is a member of NATO. Nevertheless, the public agreement does not mention nuclear weapons, nuclear sharing, or an extension of Pakistan’s nuclear deterrent to the other signatories. It also does not extend NATO protection to Saudi Arabia or Pakistan. Claims that the agreement creates a Pakistani nuclear guarantee for the three countries go beyond the available evidence.

The pact may still alter the regional balance. It links Saudi financial and political influence, Turkey’s sizeable and technologically advanced armed forces, and Pakistan’s military experience in a standing collective-defence framework. It may deter attacks by raising uncertainty about whether aggression against one member will bring assistance from the other two.

At the same time, uncertainty over the response mechanism could invite an adversary to test the pact below the threshold of a clear state attack. That possibility arose almost immediately. On 9 August, the Iran-aligned Houthis claimed a drone strike against Saudi Aramco’s Jazan refinery. Saudi Arabia confirmed that a fire occurred and was extinguished without injuries, but it did not publicly attribute the cause. Neither Turkey nor Pakistan immediately said how the agreement applied.

Iran’s official response was restrained. On 10 August, an Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman said Tehran had no reason to believe that the pact was directed against Iran and described regional reliance on local security capabilities as potentially constructive. That response lowers the immediate risk of an overt Iranian countermove, although Iran may still view an expanding Sunni-led security bloc as a longer-term constraint or encirclement effort.

The pact could reduce nuclear risk if it deters attacks and gives regional states greater confidence in collective defence. It could increase risk if proxy attacks draw the members into direct conflict, if Iran concludes that hostile states are forming a wider coalition, or if Pakistan’s nuclear status is deliberately invoked during a Gulf crisis. None of those escalatory conditions has yet been established.

The DEFCON Warning System is a private intelligence organisation which has monitored and assessed nuclear threats by national entities since 1984. It is not affiliated with any government agency and does not represent the alert status of any military branch. The public should make their own evaluations and not rely on the DEFCON Warning System for any strategic planning. At all times, citizens are urged to learn what steps to take in the event of a nuclear attack. If this had been an actual attack, the DEFCON Warning System will give radiation readings for areas that are reported to it. Your readings will vary. Official news sources will have radiation readings for your area.

For immediate updates, visit https://t.co/zLFOBRIeWy. Breaking news and important information can be found on the DEFCON Warning System community forum and on the DEFCON Twitter feed @DEFCONWSAlerts. You may also subscribe to the DEFCON Warning System mailing list. Note that Twitter updates may be subject to delays.

The next scheduled update is 1 PM, 17 August 2026. Additional updates will be made as the situation warrants, with more frequent updates at higher alert levels.

This concludes this report of the DEFCON Warning System.

text:
As the war goes on and on, the cost keeps piling up. The WSJ reported that Iran has done about $14B in damage to American bases and equipment since Operation Epic Fury began. More than 2K missile and drone strikes, 20 facilities across 8 countries damaged, at least 42 aircraft damaged or destroyed. These are just the preliminary numbers, by the way. The final numbers will likely be far higher.

The IRGC is also announcing its missiles have mid-flight course correction now and can be reassigned to a new target mid-flight to dodge U.S. air defenses.

I also have an update on the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve. It’s now fallen below 300 million barrels for the first time since 1983, down to 298.7 million after a 6.1 million barrel drop last week, leaving roughly 43 days of supply as officials draw down the stockpile to offset disruptions from the Iran War.

Things Keep Getting Worse in the Region

Yemen’s Houthis hit Bayhan this morning, killing at least 2 Saudi-backed soldiers. Other recent strikes hit Mocha (which killed at least 7 and wounded 30), Sahn al-Jinn, and Al-Wadiah. The Houthis seem unbothered by the new Saudi/Turkey/Pakistan defense pact.

Another tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was hit by Iran overnight. Occasionally a tanker makes it through the U.S.-backed corridor, but Iran is landing the overwhelming majority of hits on the Oman route. Saudi Aramco has postponed the restart of its 400,000-barrel-per-day Jazan refinery to August 30th due to attacks.

Let’s Talk About Those Alliances

Iran’s Foreign Ministry confirmed invitations for FM Araghchi and parliament speaker Ghalibaf following Pakistan’s new alliance with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, known as the “Mecca Pact.” Iran’s spokesperson says the pact isn’t a concern for them, noting it’s a sign of a regional shift away from the U.S. security umbrella. Israel’s agriculture minister Avi Dichter called the alliance “very, very problematic” for Israel, adding that Egypt will likely join too, and noting the crisis it could create due to Pakistan’s possession of nuclear weapons.

— Ben Meiselas

PROFESSOR PAPE’S VERDICT: IRAN MOVES TO HARD POWER WHILE TRUMP WATCHES HELPLESSLY

Professor Robert Pape of the University of Chicago delivered a clinical assessment this morning: the United States is no longer a player in the Persian Gulf. It is a spectator. Iran has completed its shift from survival to ambition to hard power and is now actively shaping the regional balance while Washington sits frozen in an escalation trap of its own making.

THE STRATEGIC PARALYSIS  
➡️ Trump halted the bombing campaign on July 30 and has remained locked in the bleachers ever since.  
➡️ He faces massive limits on the further use of force yet cannot accept Iran as a rising regional hegemon.  
➡️ The result is pure strategic paralysis: the field is moving, the teams are scoring, and America is watching.

IRAN’S HARD-POWER PLAY  
➡️ Tehran is deliberately keeping the Strait of Hormuz closed to almost everyone except China-bound traffic.  
➡️ Since July 20 the Houthis, Iran’s allies, have been hitting Saudi tankers and Aramco facilities, applying kinetic pressure on the Red Sea front.  
➡️ Iranian leaders have issued a maximalist list of upfront demands for any reopening of the Strait — demands that would politically destroy Trump’s presidency if met.

THE GULF REALIGNMENT  
➡️ Gulf states that once sat firmly in the American orbit are drifting toward neutrality or worse.  
➡️ America can no longer protect them, and every capital knows it.  
➡️ The new Mecca defense pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan is largely symbolic; it creates no integrated command and offers no credible deterrent to Iranian hard power.

THE EXIT TRAP  
➡️ Focusing only on an exit before the midterms narrows options further every single day.  
➡️ Pape warns the conflict is already a long war. Short time horizons make the trap tighter, not looser.  
➡️ Worse outcomes — including a path to $6 national average gasoline if Saudi oil is driven toward zero — remain fully available before November.

THE BOTTOM LINE  
Iran is no longer reacting. It is writing the next chapter of the regional order while the president who started this war finds himself with no good options and no way out of the trap he constructed.
Control has changed hands.

Can ‘Islamic NATO’ rein in both Israel and Iran?
The Mecca pact links Riyadh, Ankara, and Islamabad  in a new security framework that could reshape regional deterrence
Published 9 Aug, 2026 19:28                               | Updated 9 Aug, 2026 20:30
📷
By Murad Sadygzade, President of the Middle East Studies Center, Visiting Lecturer, HSE University (Moscow).

Telegram
📷
Turkish  President Recep Tayyip Erdogan meets with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed  bin Salman in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, on August 7, 2026 ©                 Turkish Presidency / Murat Cetinmuhurdar / Handout/Anadolu via Getty Images
The  signing of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye,  and Pakistan may eventually be remembered as one of the more  consequential geopolitical developments to emerge from the current  Middle Eastern crisis.

Signed in Mecca by Saudi Crown Prince  Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and  Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, the agreement establishes a  remarkably clear principle of collective defense, under which an armed  attack against any one of the three states is to be regarded as an  attack against all. The parties have not yet disclosed how this  commitment would operate in practice, what level of military assistance  it would automatically trigger, or whether common command and planning  mechanisms will eventually follow, but these uncertainties do little to  diminish the political significance of the arrangement. For the first  time, three of the most influential states of the broader Muslim world  have formally connected their national security in a framework that  potentially combines Saudi financial and political weight, Turkish  military-industrial power, and Pakistan’s enormous armed forces and  nuclear status.

Officials from the three countries have been  careful to avoid portraying the agreement as the birth of an aggressive  military bloc. Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz stressed that it was  not directed against any particular country, while Turkish officials  described the pact as purely defensive and underlined that it did not  cancel Ankara’s existing obligations to other partners. Saudi Deputy  Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly went even further, rejecting  the idea that Mecca represented either a sectarian military axis or the  beginning of a nuclear arms race. Such statements are understandable,  particularly at a moment when the region is already struggling with a  war involving Iran, Israel, and the United States, yet the significance  of the agreement lies less in what its signatories formally say it is  directed against than in the profound transformation of the security  environment that made such a treaty necessary in the first place.

    📷
Have Pakistan, Türkiye and Saudi Arabia just launched an ‘Islamic NATO’?Read more
The end of exclusive reliance on Washington
There is little  surprise about the emergence of this alliance. The military  confrontation that followed the US-Israeli attack on Iran on February 28  changed not only the balance of military power in the Middle East  but, importantly, the perception of security among America’s traditional  partners. Iranian missiles striking Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states,  attacks threatening regional infrastructure, and the blockade of energy  shipments exposed a basic weakness in the security model on which much  of the Gulf had relied for decades. Enormous purchases of American  weapons, the presence of US military bases, and long-standing political  alignment with Washington had been treated almost as an insurance policy  against precisely this sort of strategic vulnerability, yet when the  region descended into a wider confrontation, membership in the American  security system did not prevent Gulf countries from becoming direct  targets or protect their economies from the consequences.
This  does not mean that Riyadh is preparing to abandon Washington, nor does  Turkish participation in the agreement imply an attempt to replace NATO.  What is changing is the belief that one external security guarantor can  remain sufficient in an increasingly unpredictable international  system. The Mecca agreement represents less a break with the US than a  hedge against excessive dependence upon it, and in that sense it forms  part of a broader process of strategic ‘sovereignization’ in which  regional states are trying to diversify their defense relationships,  strengthen domestic military industries, and create arrangements that  can function even when Washington’s interests do not fully coincide with  their own. For the Gulf monarchies in particular, the conclusion is  becoming increasingly difficult to avoid – American power remains  indispensable, but American protection can no longer be regarded as  unconditional or absolute.

The institutional groundwork had  already been laid. Saudi Arabia and Pakistan concluded a mutual defense  pact last year, while their military relationship has subsequently  acquired a much more tangible character through Pakistani deployments,  fighter aircraft, drones, and air-defence capabilities in the kingdom.  At the same time, Saudi-Turkish defense ties have expanded rapidly,  Riyadh has become an important purchaser of Turkish drones, and Ankara  and Islamabad have spent years developing military cooperation through  training, naval exchanges, and defence-industrial projects. What  happened in Mecca is the political consolidation of relationships that  were already developing beneath the surface.

This is also why  Egypt should be watched closely. Over the past year, Saudi Arabia,  Türkiye, Pakistan, and Egypt have increasingly coordinated their  positions on regional security, while the gradual reconciliation between  Ankara and Cairo has removed one of the principal political obstacles  to a broader alignment among the major Sunni powers. Egyptian accession  is by no means inevitable, but strategically it would make considerable  sense, since Cairo would add the largest Arab population, one of the  region’s most substantial armed forces, and control over the Suez Canal  to an already formidable combination of Saudi capital, Turkish military  technology, and Pakistani strategic capabilities. If that happened, the  expression ‘Middle Eastern NATO’, often used rather loosely in previous  decades, would begin to describe something much more concrete.

    📷

Iranian lawmaker blasts Saudi-led defense pact with Pakistan and TürkiyeRead more
Israel and the return of regional deterrence
The most  important question, however, concerns the state against which this  emerging system of deterrence may actually matter most. The immediate  context is obviously the confrontation with Iran, yet treating the Mecca  agreement primarily as an anti-Iranian coalition would miss a deeper  transformation taking place across the region. Israel’s wars and  military operations since October 2023 have extended from Gaza into  Lebanon, Syria and Iran, while the repeated expansion of the  geographical boundaries within which Israel has been prepared to employ  force has created a growing concern among regional capitals that the  previous system of restraints has effectively collapsed. The problem  from Riyadh’s or Ankara’s perspective is not simply one particular  Israeli operation but the environment in which a single regional power  increasingly appears willing and able to strike across multiple  neighboring states without facing an organized regional counterweight.
The  Mecca framework may be more significant for Israel than for Iran. As  RUSI researcher Burcu Ozcelik noted in comments cited by Reuters, the  agreement can be understood as an attempt to create deterrence against  Israel while simultaneously counterbalancing Iranian influence, rather  than as preparation for a military confrontation with Tehran. Saudi  Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan have no obvious interest in beginning  another war with Israel, but they do have an interest in restoring  limits to unilateral military action. A bloc that combines Turkish  military capabilities and defense production, Saudi financial resources,  and Pakistani strategic depth would not need to fight Israel in order  to alter its calculations; its political value would lie in making the  potential consequences of further regional escalation less predictable  and therefore more costly.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin  Netanyahu’s office declined to comment on the agreement, but silence  should not be confused with indifference, since Israeli planners can  hardly ignore the emerging collective-defence structure linking Türkiye,  Saudi Arabia, and nuclear-armed Pakistan. Israel has long benefited  from a fragmented strategic environment in which Arab and Muslim states  possessed substantial military capabilities but remained divided by  rivalries, incompatible alliances, and competing relationships with  Washington. A gradual reduction of those divisions changes the strategic  equation even before any common military headquarters, integrated  air-defence network, or joint planning system appears.

Iran  occupies a more ambiguous position in this architecture and may  ultimately become either one of its objects of deterrence or one of its  participants. Tehran’s ability to inflict serious costs on US forces and  partners has undoubtedly strengthened its regional standing, and Saudi  Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan would have little interest in replacing  excessive dependence on Washington with acquiescence to Iranian regional  predominance. Should Iranian confidence evolve into an attempt to  establish a more explicit hegemony over the Gulf or the wider Middle  East, the Mecca framework could become a natural balancing mechanism.  Yet the opposite scenario is equally possible, because an increasingly  inclusive regional security structure might eventually offer Iran a  place within a broader system of mutual guarantees, thereby transforming  the alliance from a bloc designed to contain particular adversaries  into the foundation of a regional balance in which no single power –  Israeli, Iranian, or otherwise – could dominate the others.

    📷

A new fault line, but not a new cold war
There is another  dimension to this process that may become increasingly important,  particularly if the Mecca framework expands. Israel already participates  in I2U2 alongside India, the United Arab Emirates, and the United  States, and although I2U2 itself is not a military alliance and has  concentrated primarily on investment, technology, energy, food security,  and infrastructure, it exists alongside increasingly dense strategic  and defense relationships connecting the same states. India has built an  exceptionally close defense partnership with Israel, while New Delhi  and Abu Dhabi have also deepened military and technological cooperation,  creating the outline of another network whose strategic importance  could grow as the Middle Eastern order becomes more fragmented.
It  would nevertheless be premature to draw a neat dividing line with Saudi  Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan on one side and Israel, India, and the  UAE on the other. The UAE illustrates why the emerging order is unlikely  to resemble the rigid bloc politics of the twentieth century, since Abu  Dhabi maintains close relations with Israel and India while  simultaneously coordinating with Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, Egypt, and  Pakistan on a range of regional questions and repeatedly expressing  positions critical of Israeli actions. India presents a similar case, as  its strategic relationship with Israel coexists with increasingly  important economic, energy, and political ties with Saudi Arabia, the  UAE, and the wider Gulf. Rather than two mutually exclusive military  camps, the region may therefore be moving toward a much more complicated  structure of overlapping alignments in which states cooperate in one  sphere, compete in another, and deliberately avoid placing all their  strategic dependence on a single partner.
That very ambiguity is  one of the defining features of the emerging multipolar order. Saudi  Arabia can maintain extensive security links with the US while  purchasing Turkish military technology and building a defense pact with  Pakistan; Türkiye can remain inside NATO while creating independent  security mechanisms with non-NATO states; India can deepen its strategic  partnership with Israel without treating Saudi Arabia as an adversary;  and the UAE can cooperate with Israel while simultaneously trying to  preserve stable relations with Iran. The significance of Mecca lies not  in creating a new binary confrontation but in accelerating the erosion  of an older system in which regional states were expected to organize  themselves primarily around the geopolitical preferences of outside  powers.
For Russia and China, such a transformation naturally  creates opportunities. Countries pursuing greater strategic autonomy are  likely to diversify military procurement, technological partnerships,  investment flows, and diplomatic relationships, and Moscow retains  competitive capabilities in fields such as air defense, aviation,  missile technologies, and electronic warfare that remain highly relevant  to the security concerns of the new grouping. Beijing, meanwhile,  possesses the economic resources and political influence to support  regional arrangements that reduce the dependence of Middle Eastern  states on any single Western center. Neither Russia nor China needs  these countries to ‘change sides’; the essential feature of the new  environment is precisely that increasingly powerful states no longer  believe they should have to choose only one.

    📷

The West wants a new order, but has no plan for oneRead more

Washington’s Middle Eastern NATO – without Washington

For  decades, successive American administrations entertained various  versions of a ‘Middle Eastern NATO’, imagining a network of US partners  capable of pooling military resources, containing Iran, defending  strategic infrastructure, and ultimately reinforcing an American-led  regional order. The concept repeatedly failed because the states  expected to participate in it disagreed over threats, distrusted one  another, and remained comfortable relying on Washington as the ultimate  guarantor of their security.
Now something remarkably similar is  beginning to emerge, but under completely different political conditions  and for very different reasons. Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan are  not acting because Washington has successfully integrated them into a  new American architecture, but because the instability of recent years  has persuaded them that no external power, including the US, should  remain the sole foundation of their security. The alliance is therefore a  product not of American strategic dominance but of its declining  exclusivity, and its future expansion could produce a system in which  Washington remains important without retaining the ability to define  automatically who the region’s enemies and partners must be.
For  the Middle East itself, this development could ultimately prove  stabilizing if it evolves toward an inclusive balance rather than  another hostile bloc. The region has spent decades trapped between  external interventions, unresolved interstate disputes, ideological  confrontation, and security arrangements designed largely outside it,  while genuine stability can only emerge when the principal regional  powers develop mechanisms that make escalation costly for everyone and  compromise preferable to permanent confrontation. A system capable of  constraining Israeli unilateralism without seeking Israel’s destruction,  limiting Iranian ambitions without attempting to isolate Iran  permanently, and reducing Arab and Turkish dependence on outside  military patrons would represent something the Middle East has rarely  possessed – a security order produced primarily by the region itself.
The  American umbrella has not gone away, nor will US power vanish from the  Middle East, but the assumption that every meaningful regional security  structure must ultimately be built around Washington is beginning to  disappear. The ‘Middle Eastern NATO’ that American strategists once  imagined may indeed be taking shape, only now it is being designed by  regional powers themselves, according to their own perception of threats  and potentially with the capacity to restrain not only Iran but also  America’s closest regional ally.

• Hamas-linked reports say the IDF has begun demolishing structures near Kizan al-Najjar in southern Khan Yunis, with claims that the Yellow Line is being expanded in the area.

• Pakistan says its new defense pact with Turkey and Saudi Arabia is defensive, aimed at strengthening deterrence and not directed against any specific country.

• Additional Ukrainian strikes caused fires and outages across Russian-held territory, including Donetsk, Sevastopol, Kerch and areas near Moscow.

• Former Ukrainian commander Valerii Zaluzhnyi warned that autonomous robotic warfare could become comparable to a new form of nuclear deterrence, arguing that machines may eventually be capable of disabling entire national infrastructure systems remotely.

GLOBAL —

• The UAE says it blocked cyberattacks targeting its aviation, energy and education sectors.

• Chinese-made camera components installed on a UK Navy drone were found transmitting “heartbeat” data to an IP address in China. The equipment has since been disconnected from the internet; Britain says no sensitive information was compromised.

• Whether Iran softens any of its six conditions for reopening Hormuz.

• Any renewed attacks by Iraqi militias against Saudi Arabia.

• Whether the Houthi campaign expands beyond Yemen’s Red Sea coast.

• Signs that the U.S. blockade is putting greater economic pressure on Tehran.

• Whether Lebanon-Israel negotiations remain frozen into September.

• Any evidence supporting Iran’s claims of improved maneuverable missile capabilities.

text:
Did Pakistan, Türkiye and Saudi Arabia Really Launch an ‘Islamic NATO’?

Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye signed a joint defence agreement last Friday. Following the agreement, discussions have emerged over whether the three countries are moving toward forming a powerful military alliance similar to NATO. If such an alliance is established, it could significantly alter the military and political balance in the Middle East and surrounding regions.

The agreement comes at a time when the security situation in the Middle East has become increasingly unstable due to the ongoing war involving Iran, the United States and Israel. Iran’s retaliatory attacks on Gulf states, which have long been regarded as US allies, have exposed limitations in the existing US-led security arrangements. As a result, Arab countries are once again considering the possibility of developing alternative security mechanisms of their own.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif signed the joint defence agreement in the holy city of Mecca.

Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said that an armed attack on any one of the three countries would be considered an attack on all three. However, unlike NATO’s Article 5, the agreement does not yet clearly state whether the other countries would be obliged to take joint military action if one member came under attack.

Why Is the Agreement Important?

In the conflict-ridden Middle East, defence cooperation among three Sunni Muslim countries carries an important symbolic message. Abdulaziz Sager, chairman of the Saudi-based Gulf Research Center, said that a joint framework among the three countries could strengthen their diplomatic and defence capabilities. At the same time, it could help them develop a regional security mechanism of their own.

Each of the three countries possesses different forms of military and economic strength. Pakistan is the only Muslim-majority country with nuclear weapons. Türkiye has a powerful defence industry and the second-largest military force within NATO. Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, is one of the world’s largest crude oil exporters. It has enormous economic resources and a modern military equipped largely with US-made weapons.

However, experts say that attempts to create security alliances or establish a new balance of power in the Middle East are not new. Similar initiatives have been attempted in the past. Therefore, there is little reason to believe that the agreement will transform the entire regional situation overnight.

Muhammad Mudassir Qamar, an associate professor at Jawaharlal Nehru University in New Delhi and a Middle East expert, said it would be premature to describe the agreement as an “Islamic NATO,” a new security bloc or a new military alliance at this stage. According to him, similar efforts to establish such alliances have been made in the past as well.

What Is Behind the ‘Mecca Pact’?

The “Mecca Pact” was signed after several months of negotiations. The new defence agreement builds on a similar agreement signed between Saudi Arabia and Pakistan last year, as well as Pakistan’s growing military ties with Türkiye.

Through the agreement, Saudi Arabia is gaining a security arrangement backed by a nuclear-armed country. With the security environment in the Gulf changing amid the ongoing conflict involving Iran, Israel and the United States, the agreement is considered important for Saudi Arabia.

Several thousand Pakistani troops, 16 fighter jets, drones and a Chinese-made air defence system are already stationed in eastern Saudi Arabia. Meanwhile, Pakistan’s military has long been using Turkish-made drones and other weapons. Some of these weapons were also used during last year’s conflict with India.

The ongoing conflict in the Middle East has further complicated the region’s security environment. Despite repeated US strikes, Iran and armed groups backed by Tehran continue to carry out attacks. This has increased concerns among the Arab states of the Gulf.

Türkiye, meanwhile, is also concerned about alleged US support for Kurdish armed groups opposing the Iranian government. This issue is believed to be connected to US and Israeli plans targeting the Iranian government.

Pakistan also seeks to expand its influence in the region by leveraging its close relations with Muslim countries in the Middle East and Central Asia. The new defence agreement can therefore also be viewed as part of Islamabad’s broader strategic approach.

Reactions from Other Countries

Iran, which has long sought to maintain influence over security affairs in the Gulf region, has described the agreement as a “paper pact.” Relations between Iran and Pakistan have also not always been smooth.

Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of the Iranian Parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, said on X that Saudi Arabia should understand that simply signing a paper agreement with Türkiye and Pakistan would not guarantee its security. He argued that Saudi Arabia had also failed to achieve the security it wanted despite relying on the United States.

India is also closely watching the new agreement because of its strained relations with Pakistan and Türkiye’s support for Pakistan. Indian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that New Delhi was closely monitoring the development.

According to Jawaharlal Nehru University professor Muhammad Mudassir Qamar, the new defence cooperation is unlikely to immediately bring about any major change in India’s relations with other countries or in the broader regional defence equation. However, he said the development is worth monitoring.

In his view, the agreement could make the regional security equation more complicated for India in the coming years.

However, India’s growing relations with Saudi Arabia could serve as an important balancing factor in this regard.
