"Article 5 of the Washington Treaty has never been invoked” is factually incorrect and misleading. Hopefully, The Hindu will issue a clarification soon.

The mutual defence clause under the NATO treaty has historically been invoked only once. That was in 2001, following the 9/11 terrorist attacks. Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty states that an armed attack against one NATO member shall be considered an attack against them all.

NATO is the gold standard for international alliances; hence, any mutual defence arrangement is often compared with it. The Makkah Pact is no exception.

The real question is: Who are the intended targets or audiences of this pact—India, Iran, the USA, or the UAE? Is it a challenge to the Israel–US alliance, Iranian belligerence, or the I2U2? It is targeted at all these actors simultaneously, but to different degrees.

The core point to understand is that Saudi Arabia is the lynchpin of this pact, driven by its growing sense of insecurity, which the Saudis have been trying to address for the past decade.

In 2015, Saudi Arabia launched a Saudi-led Sunni Arab coalition of 10 countries to intervene militarily in Yemen.

Now, in the context of the Gaza and Iran wars, the situation has escalated significantly. Both Israel and Iran are emerging as the two most important poles in regional politics, while other regional powers appear to be shrinking in influence.

Two triggers are particularly important.

First, the unreliability and perceived incompetence of the United States in protecting Saudi Arabia from Iranian missiles and drones.

Second, the fratricidal tensions within the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), particularly between Saudi Arabia and the UAE, and between Saudi Arabia and Qatar.

Both Pakistan and Türkiye are peripheral powers in the Middle East and are desperately seeking to carve out a space for themselves in the emerging regional order. The real test of this pact, however, will come in a serious crisis. That test may not be far away—the entire region remains a powder keg.

text:
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement. Its central provision is deliberately NATO-like: an armed attack on one will be considered an attack on all three.

The operational details remain undisclosed. But the political direction is clear. Three authoritarian Muslim-majority states - one nuclear-armed, one inside NATO and one controlling enormous energy wealth - are constructing a security architecture independent of the United States and increasingly detached from Israel.

The Trump administration should stop confusing transactional cooperation with strategic alignment.

Turkey is the clearest example. It remains a NATO member while behaving less like a Western ally than an Islamist power using the alliance for protection and leverage. Erdoğan’s government has supported ISIS and the Muslim Brotherhood, welcomed its exiled leaders and repeatedly hosted senior Hamas officials. Erdoğan met a Hamas leadership delegation in Ankara as recently as last year, with his foreign minister and intelligence chief present. Turkey still refuses to treat Hamas as a terrorist organization.

It also suppresses the freedoms NATO supposedly exists to defend. Opposition figures are arrested, protests are crushed, foreign reporters are detained or expelled and Turkish journalists are prosecuted for criticizing Erdoğan or reporting on his government. A new cybersecurity law has expanded presidential control over the digital sphere, while Turkey ranks near the bottom of the global press-freedom index.

Turkey has also developed a growing influence campaign aimed at shaping American discourse on foreign policy. It increasingly uses English-language media ecosystems and seemingly independent online platforms to circulate narratives aligned with Ankara’s interests. As @EFischberger investigation into Clash Report demonstrated, some of these outlets operated for years with obscured ownership and staffing while building large Western audiences, only later revealing links to Turkish media networks and state-adjacent ecosystems after scrutiny. These platforms often present themselves as neutral conflict observers while amplifying positions favorable to the Turkish government and its regional agenda, including sharply anti-Israel narratives that blur into antisemitic framing. The result is a soft-power information strategy that embeds state-aligned messaging directly into U.S. media consumption, blurring the line between independent analysis and foreign influence, hardly something a friendly state would do.

Turkey also purchased Russia’s S-400 air-defence system despite explicit warnings that it could expose sensitive data on NATO aircraft. Operating or integrating the F-35 in an environment where the S-400 is present risks allowing Russian-made sensors and associated systems to collect and analyze the aircraft’s radar signatures and operational behavior, improving Russia’s ability to detect, track and eventually counter stealth platforms. That kind of intelligence gain would not remain limited to Turkey; it would ultimately erode the advantage of all F-35 operators, including the United States. The decision resulted in Turkey’s removal from the F-35 program and American sanctions. Yet Trump has now promised to lift those sanctions and is considering restoring Turkish access to the F-35, even though U.S. law prohibits a transfer while Turkey retains the Russian system. No Turkish concession disclosed so far justifies taking that security risk. One can only hope this is political lip service and that Trump has not been misled by Erdoğan’s assurances. Rewarding Erdoğan before he changes course teaches him that defiance works.

Pakistan is no more neutral.

The Trump administration has used Islamabad as an intermediary in negotiations with Iran. Pakistan and Qatar helped mediate the June 2026 memorandum intended to open a path toward ending the Iran war. But mediation is not evidence of ideological moderation or neutrality. Both Qatar and Pakistan are hardly neutral actors; in practice they have often been more aligned with Iran than with the United States, as reflected in repeated diplomatic delays, pressure for premature ceasefires, and messaging that consistently relieved pressure on Tehran at critical moments. Pakistan does not recognize Israel, US's alley in the war, and its officials do not merely criticize Israeli policy.
Pakistan’s defense minister, Khawaja Asif, called Israel “evil”, a “curse for humanity” and a “cancerous state” while his country was presenting itself as a neutral mediator. One day after signing the new defence pact, he described Israel as an “illegitimate state”, called it a threat to the entire Muslim world and demanded a “united military front” against it.

That matters. A nuclear-armed country cannot be treated as a neutral bridge while its defense minister openly calls for a military coalition against another American ally. And a pact cannot be dismissed as purely defensive when a senior signatory immediately identifies Israel as the collective enemy against which Muslims should unite.

Then there is Saudi Arabia.

Riyadh is unmistakably moving away from the strategic logic of the Abraham Accords.

The Abraham Accords offered a different regional architecture: Israel, the Gulf states, India, Europe and the United States connected through recognition, trade, energy, technology and the IMEC corridor. The Mecca pact instead places Saudi money and religious prestige behind an alternative security bloc with Turkey - the Muslim Brotherhood’s principal state patron - and Pakistan, whose government refuses to recognize Israel and whose defense minister is calling for a united military front against it.

Saudi Arabia still refuses normalization without an “irreversible” path to a Palestinian state, a coded way of calling for the destruction of the Jewish state. Trump was right to declare that the proposed American civil-nuclear agreement is off unless Riyadh joins the Abraham Accords. That condition should remain absolute. Washington should not provide advanced technology and strategic guarantees while Saudi Arabia builds a competing military structure with governments openly hostile to Israel.

Access is not allegiance. Mediation is not neutrality. Purchasing American weapons does not make a government pro-American, and NATO membership does not transform Erdoğan’s Turkey into a liberal ally.

The Mecca agreement should therefore be read as a warning. These governments will cooperate with Washington when cooperation serves them, bargain with Iran when that serves them and mobilize hostility toward Israel when that serves them.

They are not building the Abraham Accords. They are building an alternative to them.

America can work with such governments. It should never trust them as friends.

Most commentary on the pact asks the same instinctive question: Who is it aimed against? Iran? The Houthis? Israel?

The more revealing question is the opposite: 𝗪𝗵𝗼 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿?

The pact is not a conventional military bloc organized around a single external enemy. Its deeper function is to serve the internal and strategic needs of its three members. Saudi Arabia seeks security insurance, political legitimacy, and strategic autonomy. Turkey seeks to institutionalize its influence across the Gulf and Syria. Pakistan seeks financial oxygen and formal recognition as an indispensable military partner.

The symbolism is deliberate. The agreement was signed in Mecca under Mohammed bin Salman, with Erdoğan and Shehbaz Sharif present. The location embeds the pact in an Islamic political vocabulary precisely when the American-centered security architecture of the Middle East is under strain. Iran, Israel, the United States, and NATO are all absent. Those absences do not cleanly identify an enemy—they identify the intended beneficiaries.

Timing reinforces the point. Washington had discussed expanded strategic ties with Riyadh, including nuclear cooperation, but Trump linked the larger bargain to Saudi Arabia joining the Abraham Accords and normalizing with Israel. The American offer looked like security in exchange for a particular geopolitical alignment. Riyadh’s decision to lock in collective defense with Turkey and Pakistan signals that Saudi Arabia will not let its security depend on a single bargain with Washington, nor accept that it must come bundled with Israeli normalization.

Each participant extracts something concrete. For Mohammed bin Salman the pact is insurance while Vision 2030 proceeds and the kingdom hedges against American conditionality. For Pakistan it elevates long-standing financial dependence—Saudi deposits, rollovers, and oil financing—into formal strategic importance;

The agreement’s deliberate ambiguity is a feature. Ankara insists it is not directed at Iran. Obligations regarding the Houthis, Israel, or India remain undefined. That flexibility lets each side claim benefits without immediate commitment to any particular war.

The most consequential possibility is expansion. Egypt is already discussed as a potential member. What could accelerate that process? A serious violation of the status quo at Al-Aqsa Mosque. Jordan has already warned the site is in danger. A major crisis there would generate enormous political pressure across the Muslim world. Egypt, Jordan, and Syria would face strong incentives to demonstrate solidarity. 

Turkey, long positioned as a defender of Jerusalem, would sit at the center of any response. The original trilateral could rapidly become a broader Islamic security network with reach into North Africa and the Horn of Africa.

This is not a prediction that Al-Aqsa will be damaged. It is recognition that precipitating events can transform embryonic architectures overnight. The Mecca pact creates options before anyone knows which crisis will test them. Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan are placing a bet on a region in which American guarantees are less certain and regional powers are more assertive.

The danger is structural. Overlapping defense commitments, financial dependencies, and religious obligations can provide deterrence—or turn a local spark into a simultaneous test of every commitment at once. The most important question is therefore not who the alliance will fight. It is what happens if the alliance gives other countries a compelling reason to join it.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

A personal perspective on the Makkah Defense Pact

The amount of superficial & reductionist "analyses" from some think-tankers & journalists about the Makkah Pact is astonishing.

Those of us who read these "analyses" understand much less than those who don’t read anything at all.

One needs to do an "analysis fasting" (abstain from reading any take) at least for two weeks following each major event, & only focus on reading reported news (with 3kg of salt, of course).

When should one start "fasting" & skip an "analysis"? Once one encounters one of the following words or phrases: protection, security provider, sunni bloc …etc; or when strategic threats & dilemmas facing Pakistan, Türkiye, (& Egypt) are absent; or when the global dimensions are ignored.

One important element that is missing from those "analyses" is the following: Strategy is a question of options. Options are a question of cost. States enter into alliances when the latter reduce the cost on oneself and raise it on adversaries.

Another missing element is the fact that Türkiye and Egypt have asked to join the Saudi Arabian-Pakistani Military Pact signed last year. Thus a serious analyst must ask: why does Türkiye, a NATO member, feel it urgent to join the Saudi Arabian-Pakistani Military Pact?

One potential answer is that in the event of an Israeli aggression, for example, Türkiye is having doubts about U.S./NATO reliability. After all, what is NATO without the U.S.? Other NATO members are asking similar questions.

It is probable that Egypt’s request to join the Saudi Arabian-Pakistani Military Pact be accepted in the upcoming few months (if not weeks). Again, a serious analyst must ask: why does Egypt seek to join this alliance?

Another missing element is the threats Pakistan is facing. For example, the emerging Israeli-Indian "working group" poses numerous threats on different levels. There are major threats from the borders with Iran & Afghanistan with significant impact on security, economy & internal social cohesion. Furthermore, there are serious questions about Chinese ability to help. Hence, aggregating power with Riyadh & Ankara makes sense from a Pakistani point of view.

Another missing element is Saudi Arabian military capabilities. For example, among the three, the Arabian Kingdom has the most capable airforce in terms of the number of advanced, high-end combat aircrafts; technological specifics; & pilots skills (measured by many indicators, such as the number of flying hours).

Another missing element is Iran weakness. Iran is not the formidable force those "analyses" suggest it to be.

In fact, Iran is militarily weak, but is, temporarily, strategically strong. 

Here is why: 1) Iran is fighting its most existential war on its own soil, which is a devastating disadvantage; 2) its skies are an open airfield for its enemies. 3) its supply lines are in tatters. 4) its control of its borders is faltering. 5) its economy is collapsing. 6) it failed to mobilise its regional proxies as effectively as it once threatened; 7) its main leverage is not military but geography: the strait of Hormuz.

Its capacity to threaten the strait doesn’t require a capable army. A devastatingly degraded Iranian army & IRGC can still send a small group of teenagers who know how to swim to plant sea-mines & launch drones at will. The short distance makes it difficult to deal with drones & missiles, at least for now. The only way to stop that, at this moment of time, is by occupying Iranian western coasts & the U.S. seems unwilling to do that, hence the temporary, strategic leverage.

The result: teenage swimmers + U.S. unwillingness to put boots on the ground are hardly a sign of Iranian strength. The temporary, strategic leverage will never change the reality of the devastatingly degraded Iranian army & IRGC. Yes it still has missiles & drones, but so do all major powers surrounding it. It is simply a question of time before that Iranian challenge is overcome, on both levels: air defence solutions & geographic alternatives.

If we believe those "analyses", which argue that the objective is only to confront Iran, then one might say the alliance is an over-reaction.

If anything, the already weakened Iran will leave a void, & many actors (or groups of actors) will try to fill it. Could this be one of the objectives of the alliance?

Another missing element is the fact that the Makkah Pact is just the foundational step towards something bigger: a framework of aggregating the might of the three Global Middle Size Powers: Saud Arabia, Pakistan, & Türkiye. There is an emerging World Order, & participating in shaping it is chief among strategic objectives.

So far we haven’t talked about the advantages of the U.S.-Iran war for the Saudi Arabians. Yes, the war has numerous serious negative consequences for Riyadh. But are there any advantages? What are they? What role do these advantages play in motivating Pakistan, Türkiye, Egypt and others to join forces with Riyadh (starting with a military pact)?

In the 1960s, 1970s, 1980s, an Arab Quartet shouldered the responsibilities of regional peace & stability: Riyadh, Baghdad, Damascus, & Cairo. Now, Islamabad replaced Baghdad, Ankara replaced Damascus, & the global level replaced the regional level. As it was then, Riyadh is now the most central, pivotal regional capitol: the gate to the Middle East. And as a Global Middle Size Power, it is one of the few state-actors which can influence the trajectory of the emerging Global Order.

In the end, those "analyses" do NOT help us understand the Makkah Pact when they overlook strategic threats & dilemmas facing Pakistan, Türkiye, & Egypt; when they over-inflate Iranian hand, down-play its strategic weaknesses; or when they ignore Saudi Arabian military capabilities. By disregarding the global dimensions of this alliance, those "analyses" make a fatal mistake. 

The Makkah Pact is an emerging, evolving, strategic framework; the details of which will keep unfolding over next year or two; & it’s only then that we can begin to have a reliable understanding.

text:
THE MECCA PACT: HISTORY REPEATS 

On August 7, 2026, in a palace in Mecca, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan signed a piece of paper that says an attack on one is an attack on all three. 

That sentence sounds like NATO's Article 5 but it is a message, addressed to Washington, written in the language of a treaty.

Look at what each country brings, and the logic assembles itself. Turkey brings NATO's growing defence industry it has spent a decade building specifically so it never has to ask anyone's permission to arm itself again. Saudi Arabia brings capital, oil leverage, and the unmatched symbolic weight of hosting Islam's two holiest cities. Pakistan brings something the other two don't have and can't build quickly, a live nuclear arsenal and decades of conventional combat experience. Put together, three very different forms of leverage, stacked into one deterrent.

Officials insist this is "purely defensive" and "not aimed at any specific country." Watch what they don't say instead of what they do. This agreement was signed while Iran and its proxies have spent months striking Saudi energy infrastructure and Gulf shipping, following the US-Israeli war on Iran that began February 28. Saudi Arabia's own longstanding assumption that the US security umbrella would hold when it mattered has been visibly tested for the better part of a year. This pact is what a country does when it stops fully trusting that assumption but isn't ready to admit it

None of these three countries is leaving the American orbit. Turkey stays in NATO. Saudi Arabia isn't cancelling its US defense relationship. This is portfolio diversification and not a rotation out of the position. Three states that have relied on a single security guarantor are now building a second one that doesn't require Washington's approval, doesn't depend on Washington's political mood, and doesn't evaporate if a future US administration decides the Gulf isn't worth the exposure anymore.

Egypt was in earlier discussions and didn't sign. That's not nothing. Egypt is the largest Arab military, sits on the Suez Canal, and would turn a trilateral pact into a genuine quadrilateral Sunni power bloc if it joined. Whether Cairo stays out because of unresolved terms, hedging of its own, or discomfort with the Turkish or Pakistani components is the single most consequential open question this pact leaves on the table.

A Turkey with a formalized trilateral defense commitment behind it walks into every eastern Mediterranean and Aegean dispute with more diplomatic and military weight than it had a week ago, because the fundamental fact of alliance politics in this region hasn't changed since relative power matters more than stated intent, and Turkey's relative power just increased.

Regional alignments in the Middle East and eastern Mediterranean are temporary convergences of interest that dissolve the moment the interest does. Three years ago, a Turkey-Saudi-Pakistan mutual defense pact would have seemed unlikely given the diplomatic friction between Ankara and Riyadh earlier in the decade. It happened anyway, because Iranian escalation reordered everyone's priorities faster than old grievances could hold them apart.

For a country like Greece, sitting in a neighborhood where alignments can flip on eighteen months of pressure, the strategic response is to build partnerships with states whose core interests overlap durably with your own, not situationally. Right now, that shortlist is short: Israel and the UAE, the two regional actors whose energy security, containment priorities, and threat perception of revisionist regional powers line up with Athens' most consistently. Everyone else in this story is a variable. Those two, for now, are closer to a constant.

🇵🇰🇸🇦🇹🇷 The Mecca Defence Pact and the Emergence of a New Strategic Geography

🔴 1. The Core Significance
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye on 7 August 2026, may represent more than a new layer of military cooperation.
It could signal:
🇵🇰🇸🇦🇹🇷 A new phase of regional security cooperation
🌍 A shift toward a more multipolar security order
🛡️ Greater regional responsibility for regional security
🔄 Reduced dependence on external security guarantors

⚔️ 2. What Each Country Brings

🇵🇰 Pakistan
💪 One of the Muslim world's most capable conventional militaries
☢️ The only established nuclear deterrent among the three
🌊 Strategic access to the Arabian Sea
📍 Position at the intersection of South Asia, Central Asia and the Middle East
🇸🇦 Saudi Arabia
💰 Enormous financial resources
🛢️ Major energy significance
🌍 Strategic position in the Gulf
🕌 Extraordinary religious and political influence in the Muslim world
🇹🇷 Türkiye
🏭 Major defence-industrial base
🚁 Advanced drone capabilities
🚀 Missile and military technology
⚔️ Powerful armed forces
🇳🇦 NATO membership
🌍 Strategic position connecting Europe, the Middle East, the Black Sea, Caucasus and Mediterranean
🔥 Combined Strength
Together, the three countries bring:
Military Power + Nuclear Deterrence + Defence Technology + Capital + Geography + Political Influence

🌍 3. Beyond the Traditional Alliance System

For decades, Middle Eastern security has depended heavily on:
🇺🇸 The United States
🇪🇺 European security structures
🌐 External security guarantees
The Mecca pact does not necessarily reject that system.
Nor does it immediately create a NATO-style alliance.
🔑 Its deeper significance may be:
Regional powers are increasingly seeking the capacity to manage regional security without relying exclusively on an external guarantor.
This reflects a wider global trend:
🤝 Multiple strategic partnerships
🏭 Indigenous defence industries
💰 Diversified arms suppliers
🛡️ Regional security arrangements
🌐 Reduced dependence on a single great power

🗺️ 4. A Strategic Triangle Across Three Regions

The geography of the agreement is particularly important.
🇵🇰 Pakistan
South Asia → Central Asia → Arabian Sea
🇸🇦 Saudi Arabia
Gulf → Arab World → Red Sea
🇹🇷 Türkiye
Middle East → Europe → Black Sea → Caucasus → Mediterranean
🔺 Strategic Triangle
South Asia 🇵🇰 → Gulf 🇸🇦 → Eastern Mediterranean 🇹🇷
This connects three strategic theatres that have traditionally been treated separately.
Possible areas of cooperation include:
🛰️ Intelligence sharing
🪖 Military exercises
🛡️ Air defence
🚀 Missile defence
⚓ Maritime security
📡 Early-warning systems
📋 Crisis planning

🇮🇳 5. The India Dimension

For India, the agreement creates a new strategic calculation.
India has:
🇸🇦 Expanded relations with Saudi Arabia and Gulf states
🇮🇱 A deep strategic partnership with Israel
🇹🇷 A complicated relationship with Türkiye
🇵🇰 A long-standing strategic rivalry with Pakistan
⚠️ The New Calculation
The pact does not mean that Saudi Arabia or Türkiye would automatically join Pakistan in a future India-Pakistan conflict.
However:
Deterrence is not only about what allies actually do. It is also about what an adversary must consider before acting.
India may therefore have to consider whether a crisis involving Pakistan could produce:
🏛️ Diplomatic consequences
💰 Economic consequences
🛡️ Military consequences
🌍 Wider regional involvement
This could encourage India to deepen its own relationships with:
🇺🇸 United States
🇮🇱 Israel
🇫🇷 France
🇸🇦 Gulf states
🌏 Other strategic partners

🇮🇱 6. The Israel Dimension

The implications for Israel are also significant, although they should not be exaggerated.
🇹🇷 Türkiye
Strong criticism of Israeli military policy
Particularly vocal regarding Gaza and the wider region
🇸🇦 Saudi Arabia
Major Arab power
Important position on the Palestinian question
🇵🇰 Pakistan
Longstanding policy of not recognising Israel

The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, signed Friday by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, declares that an armed attack against any one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack against all.

The pact creates a formidable strategic partnership linking three states with complementary strengths: Saudi Arabia's financial and energy power, Turkey's rapidly expanding defence-industrial base and Pakistan's large armed forces and nuclear weapons capability.

It also expands a Saudi-Pakistani mutual defence arrangement concluded in September 2025, while bringing NATO member Turkey formally into a broader regional security architecture. Cooperation is expected to encompass military training, exercises, defence production and technology.

The agreement comes amid extraordinary instability across the Middle East, including the Iran conflict and disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The crisis has placed renewed pressure on Gulf governments to diversify their security relationships and strengthen their own military capabilities.

Saudi officials insist the agreement is defensive and should not be interpreted as the creation of a new military or sectarian bloc. Riyadh says the arrangement does not replace existing international partnerships.

Nevertheless, its geopolitical symbolism is difficult to ignore.

For decades, Washington has been the dominant external security power across the Gulf. The Makkah agreement suggests increasingly powerful regional states are preparing for a world in which American military protection is no longer regarded as the only foundation of their security.

Rather than signalling the immediate disappearance of US influence, the pact illustrates something more gradual: the diffusion of power.

China and Russia are expanding their diplomatic and economic reach, while Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan are developing independent centres of military influence.

The emerging international system may therefore be defined less by a single declining or dominant superpower than by overlapping alliances and regional power centres.

The Makkah pact could become one of the clearest signs yet that the multipolar world is moving from theory into geopolitical reality.

The Mecca Defence Agreement: Why India Should Care

Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan have signed a trilateral defence pact with an Article 5-style clause: an attack on one is treated as an attack on all.

This is not simply an “Islamic NATO.” Its bigger meaning is the emergence of a more autonomous regional security framework.

Why now?

• Uncertainty over the U.S. security umbrella
• Growing regional instability
• Saudi money + Turkish defence industry + Pakistani military capabilityand nuclear deterrannce
• A push for greater strategic autonomy
• Protection against cross-border and non-state threats

U.S. UNCERTAINTY
       ↓
REGIONAL INSECURITY
       ↓
Saudi capital
+ Turkish defence
+ Pakistani military depth & deterrance
       ↓
TRILATERAL SECURITY PACT
       ↓
REGIONAL AUTONOMY

Why does it matter for India?

India has long tried to keep its relations with Pakistan separate from its ties with the Gulf.

The Saudi-Pakistan defence pact makes that de-hyphenation harder.

          INDIA
            │
     ┌──────┴──────┐
     ↓             ↓
GULF AXIS       IRAN AXIS
Saudi/UAE       Iran/Chabahar
IMEC            INSTC
     │             │
     └──────┬──────┘
            ↓
     MECCA PACT
            ↓
  HARDER BALANCING FOR INDIA

1. Pakistan gets deeper into the Gulf security equation

Even if the pact is defensive and not aimed at India, Pakistan is now more closely linked to Saudi Arabia's security architecture.

2. India's deterrence calculations change

Any future India-Pakistan crisis may now carry an additional layer of uncertainty involving Saudi Arabia and Türkiye. That does not mean they would automatically intervene but the possibility matters.

3. India's connectivity strategy faces pressure

India needs both:

Chabahar → INSTC → Central Asia

and

Gulf → Saudi Arabia → IMEC → Europe

Greater Saudi-Türkiye-Pakistan alignment and growing Iran-related tensions could make balancing between these two routes harder.

Is it really like a NATO?

No.

NATO has integrated command, permanent institutions, decades of interoperability and established collective-defence structures.

The Mecca pact is still mainly a trilateral state-level framework, with different national interests and threat perceptions.

What can India do?

• Deepen strategic ties with Riyadh and seek reassurance over South Asian crises.
• Strengthen the Greece–Cyprus–UAE–India strategic axis.
• Protect its Chabahar investment and keep it focused on connectivity.

The pact does not automatically create an anti-India bloc.

But it changes India's strategic environment.

New Delhi now has to balance two increasingly important spaces: Iranian connectivity and Gulf partnerships, while Pakistan becomes more deeply connected to the Gulf security architecture.

That is the real geopolitical significance of the Mecca Agreement.

The signing of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement on August 7, 2026, inherently complicates Türkiye's geopolitical posture. By committing to a mutual defense pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia where an attack on one is treated as an attack on all Türkiye has bridged its NATO obligations with a powerful new Sunni bloc.

If a NATO member (or NATO as an alliance) were to attack Pakistan or Saudi Arabia, Türkiye would face an unprecedented treaty paradox. Here is a deep analysis of how Ankara would likely navigate this conflict, balancing its legal obligations and realpolitik survival.

The Treaty Paradox: NATO vs. The Mecca Pact

To understand Türkiye's response, we must look the legal framework of both alliances:
AllianceCore Defense ClauseTürkiye's ObligationNATO (1949)Article 5: An armed attack against one member in Europe/North America is an attack against all.Strictly defensive. Türkiye is legally bound to assist Saudi Arabia or Pakistan if they are the victims of aggression.
A Turkish official explicitly stated that the new trilateral agreement "will not alter or undermine any other alliance commitments". In diplomatic terms, this is an interpretation loophole: Ankara intends to treat the Mecca Pact and NATO as non-overlapping, defensive shields.

How Türkiye Would Respond
If a direct conflict broke out between a NATO power (such as the United States) and Pakistan or Saudi Arabia, Türkiye would likely avoid a direct, kinetic war with its Western allies. Instead, Ankara's response would be calculated and asymmetric.

1. The Institutional Veto (Preventing a "NATO" Attack)
NATO operates entirely on the principle of consensus. A unified "NATO attack" against Saudi Arabia or Pakistan is practically impossible because Türkiye sits on the North Atlantic Council (NAC). Ankara would instantly veto any alliance-wide military action against its new strategic partners. Therefore, any Western attack would have to come from a "coalition of the willing" (e.g., a unilaterally acting US-led or European-led initiative), not NATO as an institution.

2. Airspace and Base Denial
If a NATO ally launched strikes on Saudi Arabia or Pakistan, Türkiye's first actionable response would be geographical denial. Ankara would almost certainly:
Close its airspace to the attacking nation's military flights.
Suspend access to strategic bases, notably the Incirlik Air Base and the Kürecik Radar Station, preventing them from being used for intelligence gathering or power projection against Riyadh or Islamabad.

3. "Threshold" Military Support
Türkiye is highly unlikely to fire on American or French troops, as doing so could invite devastating economic sanctions and fracture NATO irreversibly. However, under the Mecca Pact, Ankara would provide immense proxy support to the defending nation:

Drones and Defense Tech: Expedited shipments of advanced UAVs, electronic warfare systems, and anti-aircraft technology.

Intelligence Sharing: Providing satellite and radar intelligence to Pakistan or Saudi Arabia to track incoming threats.

Advisors: Deploying military planners to assist in defensive maneuvers without putting Turkish uniformed soldiers on the frontline.

4. Diplomatic Weaponization

Türkiye would leverage the crisis to rally the Islamic world. Combining its military weight with Saudi Arabia's energy leverage and Pakistan's nuclear deterrence, Türkiye would attempt to force a diplomatic ceasefire. By positioning itself as the mediator between the West and the Islamic bloc, Ankara would use the crisis to assert itself as an indispensable, independent global superpower.

The Danger of a Preemptive Strike

The one scenario where Türkiye's position collapses is if Pakistan or Saudi Arabia strikes a NATO country first. Because the Mecca Pact is legally defined as "purely defensive", Türkiye would legally void its obligation to help Riyadh or Islamabad, arguing they were the aggressors. If the NATO country retaliated, Türkiye would legally be bound by NATO's Article 5 to support its Western ally, though it would likely offer only minimal, symbolic support.

Trump’s most dangerous blind spot has always been his belief that every enemy ultimately wants a deal.

He understands businessmen. He understands leverage, pressure and the desire to walk away with a win. But radical Islamist regimes and movements do not necessarily define winning the same way. For them, negotiations can be another battlefield: a way to gain time, divide opponents, secure concessions and survive until the balance of power changes.

Iran has demonstrated the problem repeatedly. Its leaders negotiated while advancing clandestine nuclear work, arming proxies and attacking Americans and their allies. Even after the latest agreement, Tehran returned to escalation rather than genuine accommodation. Trump now appears to be learning - at tremendous cost - that a signed document is worthless without verification, enforcement and the credible destruction of the capabilities being negotiated away. The latest truce has unraveled, and American forces are again striking Iranian military targets.

The lesson is larger than Iran.

It applies to Hamas. It applies to the Muslim Brotherhood. It applies to Erdoğan’s Turkey, Qatar and Ahmed al-Sharaa - the former Abu Mohammed al-Jolani - in Syria.

Then there is Taqiyya. Islamist movements have a documented record of using tactical ambiguity, temporary truces, front organizations and reassuring language for strategic purposes. 

The Holy Land Foundation trial offered a disturbing window into that world. A federal jury convicted the foundation and five leaders of providing material support to Hamas through organizations presented as charitable. Prosecutors also introduced internal Muslim Brotherhood documents describing a long-term “civilization-jihad” project and a Palestine Committee designed as "a kind of grand jihad in eliminating and destroying Western civilization from within". The convictions were for material support - not for merely possessing an ideological memorandum - but the evidence showed how humanitarian and civic structures could be exploited to sustain a terrorist movement inside the USA.

That matters because Hamas is not merely adjacent to the Muslim Brotherhood. Hamas is its Palestinian branch.
And Qatar and Turkey are not neutral referees.

Qatar has hosted Hamas leaders, amplified its propaganda ecosystem and used money and diplomacy to preserve its influence over Gaza. Turkey has treated Hamas officials as political partners rather than terrorists, while Erdoğan openly embraces the Brotherhood’s ideological world. Both countries can serve as intermediaries when necessary. But an intermediary is not automatically an honest guarantor -  and a state invested in Hamas’s survival should not be entrusted with deciding whether Hamas has genuinely been dismantled.

That is the central danger of giving Qatar and Turkey significant influence over Trump’s Gaza Board of Peace. Their objective may be to repackage Hamas, move its visible leaders aside and preserve its networks under a different name. A ceasefire that leaves Hamas’s commanders, weapons, tunnels, finances, indoctrination and coercive machinery intact is not peace. It is an intermission before the next October 7.

The same mistake infects the automatic demand for a two-state solution.

A Palestinian state created before deradicalization would not magically become moderate because diplomats called it a state. The Palestinian Authority still carries the legacy of rewarding terrorists and their families, glorifying “martyrs” and educating children through a system saturated with rejectionism. Creating another sovereign launching pad under those conditions would not solve the conflict. It would internationalize and fortify it.

Peace requires more than new borders. It requires the disarmament of Hamas, the removal of its governing apparatus, the destruction of its tunnel and financing networks, the end of “martyr” payments, and the replacement of an education system that teaches children to inherit a war. Until that transformation occurs, only Israel has both the ability and the existential incentive to ensure that Hamas does not survive underground and reappear under a new logo.
